ActionScript.creator: Gary Grossman (Macromedia)
ActionScript.history: ActionScript grew out of the simple 'actions' in Macromedia Flash; Flash 4 (1999) turned them into a small scripting language and Flash 5 (2000) renamed it ActionScript with ECMAScript-style syntax. ActionScript 3 later added classes and a new virtual machine, and the language drove Flash games and web applications through the 2000s.
ActionScript.releasedEvent: Flash 5 released, first version to call its scripting language ActionScript

Ada.creator: Jean Ichbiah (CII Honeywell Bull)
Ada.history: The US Department of Defense ran a design competition in the late 1970s to replace the hundreds of languages in its systems; Jean Ichbiah's 'Green' proposal won in May 1979. Named after Ada Lovelace, its standard was approved on her birthday and numbered 1815 for her birth year. It is used in avionics, rail and defense software.
Ada.releasedEvent: MIL-STD-1815 reference manual approved by the US Department of Defense

ALGOL 68.creator: Adriaan van Wijngaarden, Barry J. Mailloux, John E. L. Peck, Cornelis H. A. Koster (IFIP Working Group 2.1)
ALGOL 68.history: ALGOL 68 was designed by IFIP Working Group 2.1 as a successor to ALGOL 60, defined with a two-level grammar that made the report notoriously hard to read. Dijkstra, Hoare and others signed a Minority Report against it. The first implementation, ALGOL 68-R, ran at the Royal Radar Establishment in 1970.
ALGOL 68.releasedEvent: Final Report adopted by IFIP Working Group 2.1 in Munich

APL.creator: Kenneth E. Iverson (IBM)
APL.history: APL began as a mathematical notation for describing algorithms, published in Kenneth Iverson's 1962 book A Programming Language. At IBM, Larry Breed, Dick Lathwell and Roger Moore turned it into the APL\360 implementation. Its special symbol set lets whole array operations fit in one short line, and it influenced J, K and other array languages.
APL.releasedEvent: APL\360, the first implementation using APL symbols, completed at IBM

AppleScript.creator: William R. Cook and Warren Harris (Apple Computer)
AppleScript.history: AppleScript was conceived at Apple in 1989 to let users automate Mac applications by sending Apple Events. William Cook led the language design with Warren Harris as co-architect, and its English-like syntax was meant for casual users, though Cook later noted it made scripts harder to write. The first end-user version shipped with System 7 Pro in September 1993.

Arc.creator: Paul Graham and Robert Morris
Arc.history: Arc is a Lisp dialect designed by Paul Graham and Robert Morris with a focus on brevity for exploratory programming. Graham released it in a self-described semi-finished state, together with the arclanguage.org site.
Arc.releasedEvent: First public release announced by Paul Graham, with arclanguage.org

Assembly.creator: Kathleen Booth (Birkbeck College)
Assembly.history: Kathleen Booth is credited with inventing assembly language in her 1947 work with Andrew Booth on the ARC computer. David Wheeler's 'initial orders' for EDSAC in 1948 are often called the first assembler. Assembly maps readable mnemonics one-to-one onto machine instructions and remains the base layer of systems programming.
Assembly.releasedEvent: "Coding for A.R.C." by Kathleen Booth and Andrew Donald Booth

AutoHotkey.creator: Chris Mallett
AutoHotkey.history: Chris Mallett wrote AutoHotkey after his proposal to add hotkey support to AutoIt v2 got no response; he built it from scratch with AutoIt v2-style syntax and some AutoIt v3 code. It became a popular Windows tool for hotkeys, macros and UI automation; v2.0 was released in December 2022.
AutoHotkey.releasedEvent: First public beta of AutoHotkey released

AutoIt.creator: Jonathan Bennett
AutoIt.history: AutoIt was created by Jonathan Bennett in 1999 to automate repetitive Windows GUI tasks such as software installs. It grew from a simple macro tool into a full scripting language with AutoIt v3 (public beta 2002, stable 2004), and its syntax inspired AutoHotkey.

Awk.creator: Alfred Aho, Peter Weinberger, Brian Kernighan (Bell Labs)
Awk.history: Awk was written in 1977 at Bell Labs by Alfred Aho, Peter Weinberger and Brian Kernighan, and its name comes from their surnames. Built for pattern-based text processing in Unix pipelines, it was an important inspiration for Perl.
Awk.releasedEvent: Written at Bell Labs; later distributed with Version 7 Unix

Ballerina.creator: Sanjiva Weerawarana, James Clark and others (WSO2)
Ballerina.history: WSO2 introduced Ballerina in 2017 as an integration language with both textual and graphical syntax, where integration flows are described as sequence diagrams. It is aimed at cloud-native services and APIs. Version 1.0 was released on September 10, 2019.
Ballerina.releasedEvent: Preview launched at WSO2Con USA 2017 by Sanjiva Weerawarana

Bash.creator: Brian Fox (GNU Project)
Bash.history: Bash (Bourne-Again Shell) was written by Brian Fox for the GNU Project as a free replacement for the Bourne shell. Chet Ramey maintains it, and it is the default login shell on many Linux distributions.

BASIC.creator: John G. Kemeny and Thomas E. Kurtz (Dartmouth College)
BASIC.history: John Kemeny and Thomas Kurtz designed BASIC at Dartmouth so that students outside science could use the college's time-sharing computer. The first programs ran at 4 a.m. on May 1, 1964. BASIC became the standard language of 1970s and 1980s home computers.
BASIC.releasedEvent: First BASIC programs run on the Dartmouth Time-Sharing System at 4 a.m.

Batch (Windows).creator: Microsoft
Batch (Windows).history: Batch files date to DOS 1.0 in 1981, where COMMAND.COM ran a .BAT file's commands line by line and AUTOEXEC.BAT ran at startup. Later DOS versions added commands such as GOTO and IF, and cmd.exe still runs batch scripts on Windows today.
Batch (Windows).releasedEvent: PC DOS 1.0 shipped with the IBM PC, with .BAT files and AUTOEXEC.BAT

BeanShell.creator: Pat Niemeyer
BeanShell.history: BeanShell is a small Java source interpreter written in Java by Pat Niemeyer that runs Java statements and a looser scripting syntax at run time. It was bundled into tools such as Apache Ant, JMeter, jEdit and WebLogic, and was proposed for Java standardisation as JSR 274.

Boo.creator: Rodrigo B. de Oliveira
Boo.history: Rodrigo B. de Oliveira created Boo because none of the .NET and Mono languages of the time felt like Python, and he wanted a language he could extend with his own constructs. It is statically typed and runs on the Common Language Infrastructure. Boo was one of Unity's three scripting languages until support was dropped in 2014.
Boo.releasedEvent: Language created and first versions released

Brainfuck.creator: Urban Müller
Brainfuck.history: Swiss student Urban Müller designed Brainfuck while trying to write the smallest possible compiler, inspired by the 1024-byte FALSE compiler. His Amiga compiler was 240 bytes. With only eight one-character commands it is Turing-complete, and it became the best-known esoteric language.
Brainfuck.releasedEvent: Urban Müller uploaded his 240-byte brainfuck compiler (brainfuck-2.lha) to Aminet

C.creator: Dennis Ritchie (Bell Labs)
C.history: Dennis Ritchie developed C at Bell Labs from Ken Thompson's B so Unix could be written in a higher-level language; the Version 4 Unix kernel of 1973 was largely rewritten in it. Kernighan and Ritchie's 1978 book defined 'K&R C'. Its syntax shaped C++, Java, C# and many later languages.
C.releasedEvent: Ritchie's new compiler and the language renamed C at Bell Labs

C#.creator: Anders Hejlsberg (Microsoft)
C#.history: Anders Hejlsberg led C#'s design at Microsoft, where it began under the name COOL ('C-like Object Oriented Language') before trademark concerns forced a rename. It was announced with .NET in July 2000, shipped as C# 1.0 with Visual Studio .NET in 2002, and became ECMA-334 and ISO standards. It later added generics, LINQ and async/await.
C#.releasedEvent: C# announced with .NET at Microsoft's Professional Developers Conference

C++.creator: Bjarne Stroustrup (Bell Labs)
C++.history: Bjarne Stroustrup began 'C with Classes' at Bell Labs in 1979 to add Simula-style classes to C without losing its speed. Rick Mascitti suggested the name C++, first used in December 1983. It was standardized in 1998 and is used for operating systems, browsers, game engines and high-performance software.
C++.releasedEvent: First commercial release (Cfront Release 1.0) and publication of The C++ Programming Language

C--.creator: Simon Peyton Jones, Norman Ramsey
C--.history: C-- was designed as a portable assembly language for compiler writers, giving front ends control over tail calls, garbage collection and exceptions that C cannot express. Simon Peyton Jones and Norman Ramsey led the work and built the Quick C-- compiler. A dialect called Cmm is still the intermediate language inside GHC.
C--.releasedEvent: Paper 'C--: a portable assembly language' (Peyton Jones, Nordin, Oliva), Implementing Functional Languages 1997

Caché Basic.creator: InterSystems
Caché Basic.history: Caché Basic is a BASIC dialect that InterSystems added to its Caché database as an alternative to ObjectScript. Basic routines can use Caché classes and call ObjectScript functions, working directly with the database's multidimensional storage.

Ceylon.creator: Gavin King (Red Hat)
Ceylon.history: Gavin King unveiled Ceylon at a conference in China in April 2011 to address limitations of Java he had run into for a decade, such as the lack of a good way to define user interfaces. The first compiler release came that December and 1.0 in 2013. Red Hat gave it to the Eclipse Foundation in 2017 and development stopped around 2020.
Ceylon.releasedEvent: Ceylon M1 'Newton', the first official release of the compiler and runtime

Chapel.creator: David Callahan, Hans Zima, Brad Chamberlain, John Plevyak (Cray Inc.)
Chapel.history: Chapel, first the 'Cascade High Productivity Language', was created at Cray for DARPA's High Productivity Computing Systems program. It aims to make parallel programs for supercomputers as readable as serial code, with global-view arrays and locality control. It is now open source under Hewlett Packard Enterprise.
Chapel.releasedEvent: First public release (version 0.8) alongside the first Chapel tutorial at SC08

CIL.creator: Microsoft
CIL.history: CIL is the stack-based bytecode of the Common Language Infrastructure, the compile target for C#, F#, VB.NET and other .NET languages, which the runtime JIT-compiles to native code. It was called Microsoft Intermediate Language (MSIL) during the .NET betas and renamed when the CLI was standardized as ECMA-335 in December 2001.
CIL.releasedEvent: Shipped as MSIL in the first .NET Framework previews and betas

Clean.creator: Rinus Plasmeijer, Marko van Eekelen et al. (University of Nijmegen)
Clean.history: Clean grew out of research on graph rewriting at the University of Nijmegen, first described by Brus, van Eekelen, van Leer and Plasmeijer in 1987. It is a pure, lazy functional language similar to Haskell, and its uniqueness typing lets programs do destructive updates and I/O safely without monads.
Clean.releasedEvent: Paper 'CLEAN: A language for functional graph rewriting' presented at FPCA '87, Portland

Clojure.creator: Rich Hickey
Clojure.history: Rich Hickey spent about two and a half years on Clojure before releasing it in 2007. It is a Lisp on the Java Virtual Machine built around immutable persistent data structures and managed state for concurrency. Version 1.0 followed in May 2009, and it later spread to JavaScript as ClojureScript.
Clojure.releasedEvent: Initial public release by Rich Hickey

COBOL.creator: CODASYL Short-Range Committee (Jean Sammet, Howard Bromberg, Vernon Reeves, William Selden, Gertrude Tierney and others); Grace Hopper as technical adviser
COBOL.history: COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language) came out of a May 1959 Pentagon meeting that formed CODASYL to create a common business language. It drew heavily on Grace Hopper's FLOW-MATIC, and in December 1960 the same program ran on RCA and Univac machines. It still runs much of the world's banking and government record keeping.
COBOL.releasedEvent: CODASYL executive committee approved the COBOL 60 specification (printed April 1960)

Cobra.creator: Charles Esterbrook
Cobra.history: Charles (Chuck) Esterbrook developed Cobra full time, reportedly funding it with poker winnings, and released it as open source in February 2008. It runs on .NET and Mono and combines Python-like syntax with optional static typing, design by contract and built-in unit tests. The last release, 0.9.6, came out in December 2013.
Cobra.releasedEvent: Charles Esterbrook presented Cobra at the Lang.NET Symposium 2008; open-sourced under MIT on 2008-02-29

CoffeeScript.creator: Jeremy Ashkenas
CoffeeScript.history: Jeremy Ashkenas released CoffeeScript in December 2009 as a small language that compiles one-to-one into JavaScript, with syntax borrowed from Ruby, Python and Haskell. Arrow functions, classes and destructuring in ES2015 owe much to it.

ColdFusion Markup.creator: Jeremy Allaire and J. J. Allaire (Allaire Corporation)
ColdFusion Markup.history: Brothers Jeremy and J. J. Allaire built Cold Fusion in 1995 to let HTML authors connect web pages to databases. CFML uses HTML-like tags such as cfquery and cfoutput. The product passed to Macromedia in 2001 and Adobe in 2005, and open source engines such as Lucee also run CFML.

Common Lisp.creator: Guy L. Steele Jr., Scott Fahlman, Richard P. Gabriel, David A. Moon, Daniel Weinreb, Kent Pitman and others
Common Lisp.history: Common Lisp began in 1981 when ARPA manager Bob Engelmore pushed for a single Lisp to unify MacLisp successors. Guy Steele's book Common Lisp the Language (1984) served as its de facto standard until ANSI published the standard in 1994. It includes the Common Lisp Object System (CLOS) and first-class macros.
Common Lisp.releasedEvent: Publication of Common Lisp the Language (first edition) by Guy L. Steele Jr.

Component Pascal.creator: Oberon microsystems
Component Pascal.history: Component Pascal, first called Oberon/L, is a refinement of Oberon-2 by the ETH Zurich spin-off Oberon microsystems. It ships with the BlackBox Component Builder, which went open source in 2004 and is now maintained by volunteers. Gardens Point Component Pascal from QUT targets .NET and the JVM.
Component Pascal.releasedEvent: Component Pascal (originally Oberon/L) first appeared with Oberon microsystems' BlackBox Component Builder

Crystal.creator: Ary Borenszweig, Juan Wajnerman, Brian Cardiff (Manas Technology Solutions)
Crystal.history: Crystal began at Manas Technology Solutions in 2011 under the name Joy, aiming for Ruby-like syntax with static type inference and native speed. Its compiler, first written in Ruby, became self-hosting in 2013. It compiles to native code through LLVM.

Curl.creator: Steve Ward and the MIT Laboratory for Computer Science (Curl Corporation)
Curl.history: Curl began as a research project in Steve Ward's group at the MIT Laboratory for Computer Science, aiming to replace the mix of HTML, JavaScript and Java with one 'gentle slope' language for web content. Curl Corporation, co-founded in 1998 with Tim Berners-Lee and Michael Dertouzos, released commercial products from 2001; it is now owned by SCSK.
Curl.releasedEvent: Curl first appeared; Curl Corporation founded to commercialise the MIT research

Cython.creator: Robert Bradshaw, Stefan Behnel, William Stein
Cython.history: Cython began when Sage developers forked Greg Ewing's Pyrex as SageX because their patches were not accepted; Stefan Behnel merged in his own lxml fork and the result became Cython. It compiles Python-like code with optional C type declarations into C extensions and is widely used in scientific Python.
Cython.releasedEvent: First official Cython release (0.9) announced on python-announce

D.creator: Walter Bright (Digital Mars); Andrei Alexandrescu joined in 2007
D.history: Walter Bright, author of the first native C++ compiler, designed D at Digital Mars as a re-engineered C++. It added garbage collection, built-in unit tests, design by contract and compile-time function execution. D 1.0 shipped in January 2007, and D2 brought Andrei Alexandrescu's work on ranges and templates.
D.releasedEvent: First public alpha of the Digital Mars D compiler

Dart.creator: Lars Bak, Kasper Lund (Google)
Dart.history: Lars Bak and Kasper Lund of Google announced Dart in 2011 as a structured alternative for large web apps. Plans for a Dart VM in Chrome were dropped in 2015, but Dart found its main role as the language of the Flutter cross-platform UI toolkit.
Dart.releasedEvent: Dart unveiled at the GOTO conference in Aarhus and announced on the Google blog

Datalog.creator: Hervé Gallaire, Jack Minker and the logic-and-databases community; name coined by David Maier
Datalog.history: Datalog is a function-free subset of Prolog that became a field of its own after the 1977 Toulouse workshop on logic and databases; David Maier later coined the name. It is the basis of deductive databases and recursive SQL queries, and tools such as Souffle use it for static program analysis.
Datalog.releasedEvent: Logic and databases workshop in Toulouse organised by Hervé Gallaire and Jack Minker

Dylan.creator: Apple Computer (Apple Cambridge); syntax by Michael Kahl
Dylan.history: Dylan, short for DYnamic LANguage, was created at Apple in the early 1990s for the Newton PDA, combining Lisp's dynamism with Common Lisp's object system. It switched from prefix s-expressions to an ALGOL-like syntax. Apple dropped it in 1995, and Harlequin's compiler lives on as Open Dylan.
Dylan.releasedEvent: Apple published the first Dylan language description

Eiffel.creator: Bertrand Meyer (Interactive Software Engineering, now Eiffel Software)
Eiffel.history: Bertrand Meyer designed Eiffel in 1985 at Interactive Software Engineering to make commercial software more reliable, and showed it at the first OOPSLA in 1986. It introduced Design by Contract, with preconditions, postconditions and class invariants. Eiffel became ECMA standard 367 in 2005.
Eiffel.releasedEvent: First Eiffel compiler released by Interactive Software Engineering

Elixir.creator: José Valim (Plataformatec)
Elixir.history: José Valim started Elixir in early 2011 to bring more extensibility and productivity to the Erlang VM (BEAM). After an early version wrapped every Erlang module, he rewrote it, and Plataformatec sponsored the work. It keeps full compatibility with Erlang libraries and is used for web systems such as the Phoenix framework, telecoms and finance.
Elixir.releasedEvent: Elixir v0.5.0 released, the first release of the rewritten language

Elm.creator: Evan Czaplicki
Elm.history: Elm began as Evan Czaplicki's 2012 senior thesis at Harvard on functional reactive programming for GUIs, shipped with a compiler and an online editor. It compiles to JavaScript and is known for friendly compiler errors and for having no runtime exceptions in practice. Its model-view-update pattern, the Elm Architecture, influenced front-end libraries such as Redux.
Elm.releasedEvent: Evan Czaplicki's Harvard thesis 'Elm: Concurrent FRP for Functional GUIs', with a working compiler and online editor at elm-lang.org

Erlang.creator: Joe Armstrong, Robert Virding, Mike Williams (Ericsson)
Erlang.history: Erlang was developed at the Ericsson Computer Science Laboratory to program telephone switches, first as an interpreter written in Prolog that proved too slow for products. It was built for massive concurrency, fault tolerance and hot code loading, and the AXD301 switch held over a million lines of it. Ericsson released Erlang/OTP as open source in December 1998.
Erlang.releasedEvent: First Prolog-based implementation at the Ericsson Computer Science Laboratory

F#.creator: Don Syme (Microsoft Research)
F#.history: Don Syme at Microsoft Research Cambridge built F# as an implementation of the core of OCaml for .NET, first released quietly in 2002; a pre-release of F# 1.0 followed in January 2005. It brought type inference, pattern matching and algebraic data types to .NET, shipped in Visual Studio 2010, and was open sourced in 2010.
F#.releasedEvent: F# v0.1 released near-silently on Microsoft Research's site as part of the ILX project

Factor.creator: Slava Pestov
Factor.history: Slava Pestov created Factor in 2003 as a scripting language for a Java game. The first implementation ran on the JVM; in 2004 it moved to a native runtime with a small C core, and the rest is written in Factor itself. It is a stack-based concatenative language with dynamic typing, macros and an interactive environment.
Factor.releasedEvent: Development began (first implementation, JFactor, on the JVM)

Forth.creator: Charles H. Moore
Forth.history: Charles H. Moore developed Forth from 1968 as a personal system; its name is 'fourth' cut to five letters, because the IBM 1130 he used allowed only five-character identifiers. In 1971 he built a complete stand-alone Forth to control the radio telescope at NRAO's Kitt Peak site. It is a stack-based, concatenative language with a tiny, extensible core.
Forth.releasedEvent: Forth first used by programmers other than Moore

Fortran.creator: John Backus (IBM)
Fortran.history: John Backus proposed Fortran (Formula Translation) to IBM in late 1953, and his team delivered the first compiler for the IBM 704 in April 1957 after a reference manual in October 1956. As the first widely used high-level language it showed that compiled code could rival hand-written assembly, and it remains central to scientific and numerical computing.
Fortran.releasedEvent: First FORTRAN compiler delivered for the IBM 704

Gambas.creator: Benoît Minisini
Gambas.history: Benoît Minisini started Gambas (Gambas Almost Means BASIC) in 1999, frustrated by the bugs and inconsistencies of Visual Basic. It is a free IDE and object-oriented BASIC interpreter for Linux in the style of Visual Basic, and the word 'gambas' means prawns, hence its logo. Version 1.0 came out in January 2005.
Gambas.releasedEvent: Project started / first release per Wikipedia

Genie.creator: Jamie McCracken
Genie.history: Genie was designed by Jamie McCracken in 2008 as a Python-like alternative syntax for the Vala compiler. It compiles to C targeting the GObject system, and Genie and Vala code can be mixed in one project, which made it a light way to write GNOME applications.
Genie.releasedEvent: Jamie McCracken's post 'Introducing Genie - the smart programming language'

Go.creator: Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike, Ken Thompson (Google)
Go.history: Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike and Ken Thompson began sketching Go on a whiteboard at Google on 21 September 2007, frustrated that no mainstream language offered fast compilation, fast execution and ease of programming together. Google open-sourced it on 10 November 2009. It has a small syntax, fast builds and goroutines with channels for concurrency.
Go.releasedEvent: Go announced and open-sourced by Google

Gosu.creator: Scott McKinney (Guidewire Software)
Gosu.history: Gosu began around 2002 inside Guidewire Software as GScript, a scripting language for its insurance applications, and lead developer Scott McKinney grew it into a general-purpose JVM language. Guidewire released it to the public in November 2010. It adds structural typing, extension methods, closures and an open type system to the Java platform.
Gosu.releasedEvent: Gosu 0.7 beta released to the public by Guidewire

Groovy.creator: James Strachan
Groovy.history: James Strachan announced Groovy on his blog in August 2003 as a dynamic language for the JVM with Java-like syntax and ideas from Python, Ruby and Smalltalk. It went through the Java Community Process as JSR 241, reached 1.0 in January 2007, added optional static compilation in 2.0 and became an Apache project in 2015.
Groovy.releasedEvent: James Strachan's blog post "Groovy - the birth of a new dynamic language for the Java platform"

Hack.creator: Facebook (Julien Verlaguet, Alok Menghrajani et al.)
Hack.history: Hack was built at Facebook for the HHVM runtime as a dialect of PHP with gradual static typing, generics, nullable types and collections. Facebook migrated nearly all of its PHP code to Hack before releasing it as open source in March 2014. Its type checker is written in OCaml and runs as a background server.
Hack.releasedEvent: Hack announced and open-sourced by Facebook

Haskell.creator: Haskell Committee (report editors Paul Hudak and Philip Wadler)
Haskell.history: A committee formed at the FPCA '87 conference to define one open standard for lazy, purely functional languages, and the Haskell 1.0 Report, edited by Paul Hudak and Philip Wadler, appeared on 1 April 1990. Named after logician Haskell Curry, it has lazy evaluation, static typing and type classes.

Haxe.creator: Nicolas Cannasse
Haxe.history: Nicolas Cannasse started haXe on 22 October 2005 as a successor to his MTASC ActionScript compiler; the beta came out in February 2006 and 1.0 in May 2006. One code base compiles to many targets, including JavaScript, C++, C#, Java, Python and PHP, which makes it popular for cross-platform games.
Haxe.releasedEvent: haXe beta released (targets AVM bytecode and Neko)

Holy C.creator: Terry A. Davis
Holy C.history: HolyC is the C-like language Terry A. Davis wrote for his own operating system, released in 2005 as J Operating System and later renamed LoseThos, SparrowOS and finally TempleOS. Formerly called C+, it is compiled just in time and also serves as the system's shell, running in ring 0 alongside the rest of TempleOS.
Holy C.releasedEvent: First release of Terry Davis's operating system (as J Operating System), whose systems language later became HolyC

HTML.creator: Tim Berners-Lee (CERN)
HTML.history: Tim Berners-Lee created HTML at CERN for sharing scientific documents, basing it on SGML and adding hypertext links. His "HTML Tags" document of late 1991 described 18 elements. Berners-Lee and Dan Connolly drafted the first IETF specification in 1993, and HTML 2.0 became RFC 1866 in 1995.
HTML.releasedEvent: "HTML Tags", the first public description of HTML, posted by Tim Berners-Lee in late 1991

Icon.creator: Ralph Griswold (University of Arizona)
Icon.history: Ralph Griswold, a designer of SNOBOL at Bell Labs, designed Icon at the University of Arizona from 1977 as a successor to SNOBOL4, and it was first released in 1979. It is known for goal-directed evaluation, where expressions can succeed, fail or generate several results, which makes string scanning concise.
Icon.releasedEvent: First release of Icon by the University of Arizona

Inform 7.creator: Graham Nelson
Inform 7.history: Inform 7 is Graham Nelson's 2006 system for writing interactive fiction, in which source text reads like English sentences describing rooms, things and rules. It was announced as a public beta on rec.arts.int-fiction in April 2006, and it compiles through Inform 6 to the Z-machine or Glulx formats.

Io.creator: Steve Dekorte
Io.history: Steve Dekorte began Io in March 2002 as a minimal prototype-based language, inspired by Smalltalk, Self, NewtonScript, Act1, Lisp and Lua. Everything is an object and every action is a message, and code is a message tree that can be inspected at runtime. It has actors, coroutines and futures for concurrency.
Io.releasedEvent: First public releases and programming guide distributed via the iolanguage mailing list

J.creator: Kenneth E. Iverson, Roger Hui
J.history: J is an array programming language designed by Kenneth E. Iverson and Roger Hui as a successor to Iverson's APL. It uses only plain ASCII characters instead of APL's special symbols. Jsoftware has published it as free and open-source software under the GPLv3 since 2011.
J.releasedEvent: First implementation of J by Iverson and Hui

Java.creator: James Gosling (Sun Microsystems)
Java.history: James Gosling started the language in June 1991 at Sun Microsystems as Oak, named after a tree outside his office, and it was renamed Java after the coffee. Sun promoted it with 'Write Once, Run Anywhere': programs compile to bytecode that runs on the Java Virtual Machine. It became a mainstay of enterprise servers and Android apps.
Java.releasedEvent: Java and HotJava formally announced by Sun at SunWorld '95; JDK 1.0 followed on 1996-01-23

JavaScript.creator: Brendan Eich (Netscape)
JavaScript.history: Brendan Eich wrote the first version in 10 days in May 1995 at Netscape to add interactivity to web pages. Called Mocha, then LiveScript, it was renamed JavaScript for its December 1995 announcement with Sun. Standardized as ECMAScript, it runs in every web browser and on servers through Node.js.
JavaScript.releasedEvent: Netscape and Sun jointly announce JavaScript (earlier shipped as LiveScript in the Navigator 2.0 beta, September 1995)

Julia.creator: Jeff Bezanson, Stefan Karpinski, Viral B. Shah, Alan Edelman
Julia.history: Jeff Bezanson, Stefan Karpinski, Viral B. Shah and Alan Edelman began Julia in 2009 and announced it in February 2012. They wanted to solve the 'two-language problem': the ease of Python, R or MATLAB with speed close to C. It is used widely in scientific and numerical computing.
Julia.releasedEvent: 'Why We Created Julia' blog post announcing the language

K.creator: Arthur Whitney (Kx Systems)
K.history: K is a terse array programming language designed by Arthur Whitney, who earlier worked on APL and A+. He founded Kx Systems in 1993 and licensed K exclusively to Union Bank of Switzerland for trading systems until 1997. K underlies the kdb+ database and its q language, which are used in finance.
K.releasedEvent: First appearance; Kx Systems founded to sell K to UBS

Kotlin.creator: JetBrains (lead designer Andrey Breslav)
Kotlin.history: JetBrains unveiled Kotlin in July 2011 as a concise, null-safe language fully interoperable with Java, named after Kotlin Island near Saint Petersburg. Version 1.0 shipped in 2016. Google added official Android support in 2017 and declared Kotlin its preferred language for Android development in 2019.
Kotlin.releasedEvent: JetBrains unveils Project Kotlin (at the JVM Language Summit); Kotlin 1.0 released 2016-02-15

Lasso.creator: Vince Bonfanti, Kyle Jessup (Blue World Communications)
Lasso.history: Lasso began in 1995 as Vince Bonfanti's CGI connector for publishing FileMaker Pro databases on the web. Blue World Communications bought the code, and Kyle Jessup, its lead programmer, built Lasso 1.0 and later grew it into a general-purpose object-oriented language. Claris licensed it as CDML for FileMaker Pro 4.0.
Lasso.releasedEvent: Lasso 0.1, a FileMaker Pro CGI by Vince Bonfanti; Lasso 1.0 released 1996-09-27

Limbo.creator: Sean Dorward, Phil Winterbottom, Rob Pike (Bell Labs)
Limbo.history: Limbo was designed by Sean Dorward, Phil Winterbottom and Rob Pike at Bell Labs as the application language of the Inferno operating system. It has channel-based concurrency drawn from CSP, Newsqueak and Alef, and compiles to portable bytecode for the Dis virtual machine. It influenced Go.
Limbo.releasedEvent: First appeared with the Inferno operating system

LiveScript.creator: George Zahariev (fork of Satoshi Murakami's Coco)
LiveScript.history: LiveScript is a fork of Coco, itself a fork of Jeremy Ashkenas's CoffeeScript, renamed and developed by George Zahariev. It compiles to JavaScript and adds functional features such as currying, piping, function composition and pattern matching. Its name nods to JavaScript's own name before December 1995.
LiveScript.releasedEvent: Coco fork renamed to LiveScript in the official repository

Logo.creator: Wally Feurzeig, Seymour Papert, Cynthia Solomon (BBN)
Logo.history: Logo was created in 1967 at BBN in Cambridge, Massachusetts by Wally Feurzeig, Seymour Papert and Cynthia Solomon to teach children to think mathematically. The name comes from the Greek logos. Its turtle, first a floor robot and later a screen cursor, made turtle graphics a lasting way to teach programming.
Logo.releasedEvent: Created at Bolt, Beranek and Newman (BBN); first implementation 'Ghost' in Lisp on a PDP-1

Logtalk.creator: Paulo Moura
Logtalk.history: Paulo Moura started Logtalk 2 in January 1998 at the University of Coimbra as an object-oriented extension of Prolog, after a 1995 experiment in computational reflection under the same name. It adds objects, protocols and categories while running on top of many Prolog compilers. Logtalk 3 followed in 2015.
Logtalk.releasedEvent: First public beta of Logtalk 2 (alpha for registered users in July 1998; first stable 2.0 on 1999-02-09)

LOLCODE.creator: Adam Lindsay (Lancaster University)
LOLCODE.history: Adam Lindsay, a researcher at Lancaster University's Computing Department, created LOLCODE in 2007 as a joke based on the lolspeak captions of LOLcats memes. Programs open with HAI and close with KTHXBYE. The loose specification inspired many implementations, including a PHP parser by Jeff Jones, a .NET compiler and the C interpreter lci.
LOLCODE.releasedEvent: Adam Lindsay put the LOLCODE specification wiki online (cited as 25 May 2007)

Lua.creator: Roberto Ierusalimschy, Luiz Henrique de Figueiredo, Waldemar Celes (TeCGraf, PUC-Rio)
Lua.history: Lua was created at TeCGraf, PUC-Rio in Brazil, for Petrobras projects, by merging two in-house languages, the data-entry language DEL and the configuration language SOL. Lua 1.0 was running in July 1993 but never released publicly. It is a small, embeddable scripting language widely used for game scripting.
Lua.releasedEvent: Lua 1.1 released by ftp, the first public release (Lua 1.0 ran internally from July 1993)

Maple.creator: Keith Geddes, Gaston Gonnet et al. (Symbolic Computation Group, University of Waterloo)
Maple.history: Maple began at a late 1980 meeting at the University of Waterloo, where researchers chose to build their own computer algebra system for cheap machines instead of buying hardware to run Macsyma. A first limited version took three weeks. Waterloo Maple Inc. (Maplesoft) was founded in 1988 to sell it.
Maple.releasedEvent: Fuller versions of Maple entered mainstream use at Waterloo (project began late 1980)

MATLAB.creator: Cleve Moler; commercial version by Jack Little and Steve Bangert (MathWorks)
MATLAB.history: Cleve Moler wrote the original Fortran MATLAB (Matrix Laboratory) at the University of New Mexico in the late 1970s so students could use LINPACK and EISPACK without writing Fortran. Jack Little and Steve Bangert rewrote it in C, and MathWorks launched PC-MATLAB in December 1984. It is used for numerical computing, engineering and data plotting.
MATLAB.releasedEvent: PC-MATLAB, the first commercial MATLAB, debuted at the IEEE Conference on Decision and Control in Las Vegas

Mercury.creator: Zoltan Somogyi, Fergus Henderson, Thomas Conway (University of Melbourne)
Mercury.history: Mercury was developed at the University of Melbourne by Fergus Henderson, Thomas Conway and Zoltan Somogyi, under Somogyi's supervision, to apply software engineering discipline to logic programming. It keeps Prolog's syntax but adds strong type, mode and determinism systems. The compiler is written in Mercury and uses C as a portable assembler.
Mercury.releasedEvent: First version of Mercury released by the University of Melbourne

Nim.creator: Andreas Rumpf
Nim.history: Andreas Rumpf began the language in 2005 as Nimrod and made the first public release in 2008. It is a statically typed language that compiles to C, C++ and JavaScript, with Python-like indentation syntax and a macro system. It was renamed Nim in December 2014 and reached version 1.0 in September 2019.
Nim.releasedEvent: Nimrod 0.6.0 released, the first version of the compiler able to compile itself

Objective-C.creator: Brad Cox and Tom Love (Productivity Products International)
Objective-C.history: Brad Cox and Tom Love met Smalltalk at ITT in the early 1980s, and Cox wrote a C preprocessor called OOPC that added Smalltalk-style messaging; it was renamed Objective-C. Cox described it in his 1986 book Object-Oriented Programming: An Evolutionary Approach. NeXT licensed it in 1988, and it became the main language of NeXTSTEP, macOS and iOS until Swift.
Objective-C.releasedEvent: First release by Productivity Products International (later Stepstone)

OCaml.creator: Xavier Leroy, Jérôme Vouillon, Didier Rémy, Damien Doligez (INRIA)
OCaml.history: Objective Caml added objects and classes, by Didier Rémy and Jérôme Vouillon, to Xavier Leroy's Caml Special Light, which already had a module system and native-code compiler. It descends from the Caml family of ML dialects developed at INRIA since the 1980s and was renamed OCaml in 2011.

Octave.creator: John W. Eaton
Octave.history: Octave was conceived around 1988 as companion software for a chemical reactor design textbook by James Rawlings and John Ekerdt, and John W. Eaton began full-time development in 1992. It is named after Octave Levenspiel, a former professor known for quick back-of-the-envelope calculations, not the musical interval. It is a free, largely MATLAB-compatible numerical environment.

Pascal.creator: Niklaus Wirth (ETH Zurich)
Pascal.history: Niklaus Wirth left the ALGOL X committee in 1968 and refined his ALGOL W into Pascal, named after Blaise Pascal, as a language for teaching structured programming. The first compiler, for the CDC 6000, ran in mid-1970. Pascal was used on the Apple Lisa and early Macintosh and led to UCSD Pascal, Turbo Pascal and Delphi.
Pascal.releasedEvent: First compiler operational at ETH Zurich and language published

Perl.creator: Larry Wall
Perl.history: Larry Wall wrote Perl in 1987 while working at Unisys, to make report processing on Unix easier. Its text processing and regular expressions made it the main language of early web CGI scripts. Perl 5 (1994) added objects, references and modules, and CPAN followed in 1995.

PHP.creator: Rasmus Lerdorf
PHP.history: Rasmus Lerdorf wrote Personal Home Page Tools in 1994 as C CGI binaries to track visits to his online resume, and released the source in June 1995. It became PHP/FI, and the 1998 rewrite by Andi Gutmans and Zeev Suraski, PHP 3, renamed it the recursive PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor. It became one of the most widely used server-side web languages.
PHP.releasedEvent: Rasmus Lerdorf publicly released the source of Personal Home Page Tools

PowerShell.creator: Jeffrey Snover, Bruce Payette, James Truher (Microsoft)
PowerShell.history: Jeffrey Snover laid out the design in his 2002 Monad Manifesto, and Microsoft renamed Monad to Windows PowerShell before the 1.0 release in 2006. Commands pass .NET objects instead of text between pipeline stages. It became cross-platform and open source in 2016.
PowerShell.releasedEvent: Windows PowerShell 1.0 released to the web

Prolog.creator: Alain Colmerauer and Philippe Roussel (Aix-Marseille University)
Prolog.history: Alain Colmerauer and Philippe Roussel created Prolog in Marseille in 1972, building on Robert Kowalski's procedural reading of Horn clauses; Roussel's wife suggested the name, from programmation en logique. David H. D. Warren's DEC-10 compiler set the Edinburgh syntax most systems use. Japan's Fifth Generation project built on it, and IBM Watson used it for parsing.
Prolog.releasedEvent: First Prolog system built in Marseille

Python.creator: Guido van Rossum (CWI)
Python.history: Guido van Rossum began implementing Python in December 1989 at CWI in the Netherlands as a successor to the ABC language, and named it after Monty Python's Flying Circus. It emphasises readability and significant indentation, and is now one of the most widely used languages, especially for scripting, data science and machine learning.

R.creator: Ross Ihaka and Robert Gentleman (University of Auckland)
R.history: R was started by Ross Ihaka and Robert Gentleman at the University of Auckland to teach introductory statistics, and its syntax follows the S language from Bell Labs. It became a GNU project in 1997, reached version 1.0 on 29 February 2000, and is now a standard environment for statistical computing and plotting.
R.releasedEvent: Binary posted to StatLib and announced on the s-news mailing list

Racket.creator: PLT (Matthias Felleisen, Matthew Flatt, Robert Bruce Findler, Shriram Krishnamurthi et al.)
Racket.history: Racket began in January 1995 when Matthias Felleisen's group set out to build a language, curriculum and IDE for teaching programming; Matthew Flatt built the MrEd and MzScheme runtime. Known as PLT Scheme, it was renamed Racket with version 5.0 in June 2010, and it is designed as a platform for creating new languages.
Racket.releasedEvent: PLT project begun in January 1995; MrEd 0.7 (1995-05-10) is the oldest entry in Racket's HISTORY files

Raku.creator: Larry Wall and the Raku community
Raku.history: Raku began as Perl 6, announced by Larry Wall at the State of the Onion talk on 19 July 2000 as a redesign of Perl. After fifteen years of design and several implementations, the 6.c 'Christmas' version shipped in December 2015, and the language was renamed Raku in October 2019 to mark it as distinct from Perl 5.
Raku.releasedEvent: Perl 6.c 'Christmas', the first official release of the language

Rexx.creator: Mike Cowlishaw (IBM)
Rexx.history: Mike Cowlishaw began Rexx (Restructured Extended Executor) in his own time at IBM on 20 March 1979, writing the interpreter in assembly language, to make a highly readable scripting language for mainframes. It was described publicly at the SHARE 56 conference in 1981, shipped as an IBM product from 1982 and was supplied with VM/SP Release 3 and later.
Rexx.releasedEvent: First shipped as an IBM product (development began 1979-03-20; first public description at SHARE 56 in 1981)

Ruby.creator: Yukihiro Matsumoto
Ruby.history: Yukihiro 'Matz' Matsumoto created Ruby in Japan, naming it in an online chat in February 1993, and blended ideas from Perl, Smalltalk, Eiffel, Ada and Lisp. He aimed to make programmers happy and the language 'natural, not simple'. Ruby on Rails made it a staple of web development in the 2000s.
Ruby.releasedEvent: Ruby 0.95 announced on Japanese domestic newsgroups

Rust.creator: Graydon Hoare (Mozilla)
Rust.history: Rust began in 2006 as a personal project of Mozilla employee Graydon Hoare, and Mozilla began sponsoring it in 2009. It reached its first stable release, 1.0, in May 2015. Rust guarantees memory safety without a garbage collector through ownership and a borrow checker, and is used widely for systems and infrastructure software.
Rust.releasedEvent: Rust 0.1 released by Mozilla (Rust 1.0, the first stable release, followed on 2015-05-15)

Scala.creator: Martin Odersky (EPFL)
Scala.history: Scala was designed by Martin Odersky at EPFL from 2001 as a successor to his earlier Funnel language. It runs on the JVM and combines functional and object-oriented programming in a statically typed language meant to scale from small scripts to large systems. Version 2.0 followed in 2006.
Scala.releasedEvent: Martin Odersky announced the first implementation on the Haskell mailing list

Scheme.creator: Guy L. Steele Jr. and Gerald Jay Sussman (MIT AI Lab)
Scheme.history: Gerald Jay Sussman and Guy L. Steele Jr. created Scheme at the MIT AI Lab in 1975 and described it in a series of memos now known as the Lambda Papers. As a minimalist Lisp dialect, it pioneered lexical scoping, block structure and first-class continuations, influencing compiler theory.
Scheme.releasedEvent: MIT AI Memo 349, "SCHEME: An Interpreter for Extended Lambda Calculus", published

Shakespeare.creator: Karl Wiberg and Jon Åslund
Shakespeare.history: Karl Wiberg and Jon Åslund designed the Shakespeare Programming Language late one February night in 2001, for a programming assignment due at nine the next morning. Programs read like plays: variables are characters, values come from insults and compliments, and stage directions control flow. The original compiler translates SPL to C.
Shakespeare.releasedEvent: Language designed in one night as a university programming assignment

Smalltalk.creator: Alan Kay, Dan Ingalls, Adele Goldberg and others (Xerox PARC)
Smalltalk.history: Smalltalk began with a bet in September 1972: Alan Kay claimed a message-passing language could be defined in a page of code, and days later Dan Ingalls had it running in BASIC on a Data General Nova. Developed at Xerox PARC with Adele Goldberg and others, it became a purely object-oriented system with a graphical environment; Smalltalk-80 was the first public version.
Smalltalk.releasedEvent: First Smalltalk-72 interpreter, written by Dan Ingalls on a Data General Nova in fall 1972

SQL.creator: Donald D. Chamberlin and Raymond F. Boyce (IBM)
SQL.history: Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce designed SEQUEL at IBM's San Jose lab to query data in Edgar F. Codd's relational model, and published it in May 1974. The name was later shortened to SQL, apparently over a trademark conflict. Oracle V2 and IBM System/38 shipped commercial implementations in 1979, and SQL became an ANSI and ISO standard.
SQL.releasedEvent: Paper "SEQUEL: A Structured English Query Language" presented at the ACM SIGFIDET workshop, Ann Arbor

Swift.creator: Chris Lattner (Apple)
Swift.history: Chris Lattner started Swift in secret in July 2010, and it became a major focus of Apple's developer tools group in 2013. Apple unveiled it at WWDC in June 2014 as a safer, faster successor to Objective-C for iOS and OS X apps, and open-sourced it in December 2015.
Swift.releasedEvent: Swift announced at Apple's WWDC 2014 keynote, with a beta for developers

Tcl.creator: John Ousterhout (University of California, Berkeley)
Tcl.history: John Ousterhout conceived Tcl in 1987 on sabbatical at DEC and started it in early 1988 at Berkeley as a reusable command language for interactive tools. Everything in Tcl is a string. After his 1990 USENIX paper it spread quickly, helped by the Tk GUI toolkit released in 1991.
Tcl.releasedEvent: Ousterhout's Tcl paper at the Winter USENIX Conference; source made freely available on Berkeley's FTP site around then

TypeScript.creator: Anders Hejlsberg (Microsoft)
TypeScript.history: TypeScript was developed at Microsoft under Anders Hejlsberg, designer of Turbo Pascal, Delphi and C#, and unveiled in October 2012 after two years of internal work. It is a typed superset of JavaScript that compiles to plain JavaScript, so any JavaScript program is already valid TypeScript, and it is now widely used for large web applications.
TypeScript.releasedEvent: TypeScript 0.8 unveiled as an early preview in S. Somasegar's Microsoft blog post

VBA.creator: Microsoft
VBA.history: VBA (Visual Basic for Applications) debuted in Microsoft Excel 5.0 in 1993, based on Visual Basic 3.0. It embeds Visual Basic in Microsoft Office applications for automation, custom macros and spreadsheet scripting, and from 1996 Microsoft also licensed it to other software vendors.
VBA.releasedEvent: Shipped in Microsoft Excel 5.0, the first application to include VBA

VBScript.creator: Microsoft
VBScript.history: VBScript (Visual Basic Scripting Edition) was released by Microsoft in 1996. It is an Active Scripting language modeled on Visual Basic, used for Windows administration, classic ASP pages and client-side scripting in Internet Explorer. Microsoft has since deprecated it.
VBScript.releasedEvent: First appeared in 1996 (Wikipedia gives May 1996); shipped with Internet Explorer 3.0 in August 1996

Verilog.creator: Phil Moorby (Gateway Design Automation)
Verilog.history: Phil Moorby designed Verilog at Gateway Design Automation in 1983-84, a startup he joined with Prabhu Goel and Chi-Lai Huang, and its first simulator shipped in early 1985. Cadence bought Gateway, opened the language, and it became IEEE 1364-1995. It is used to model and design digital logic, microprocessors and ASICs.
Verilog.releasedEvent: First Verilog simulator brought to market by Gateway Design Automation in early 1985

VHDL.creator: US Department of Defense (Intermetrics, IBM and Texas Instruments)
VHDL.history: VHDL (VHSIC Hardware Description Language) was commissioned by the US Department of Defense to document the behaviour of ASICs in its equipment. Intermetrics, IBM and Texas Instruments developed it from 1983, published version 7.2 in 1985, and it became IEEE 1076 in 1987. It is a strongly typed language used to simulate and synthesize digital circuits and FPGA designs.

Visual Basic .NET.creator: Microsoft
Visual Basic .NET.history: Visual Basic .NET was launched by Microsoft in February 2002, with Visual Studio .NET, to move the classic Visual Basic language to the .NET Framework. It is a fully object-oriented language that shares the common language runtime (CLR) with C#, and it broke compatibility with VB6 code.
Visual Basic .NET.releasedEvent: Launched as part of Visual Studio .NET and the .NET Framework at VSLive! 2002

WebAssembly Text.creator: W3C WebAssembly Community Group
WebAssembly Text.history: The WebAssembly Text format (WAT) is the human-readable form of WebAssembly, mixing S-expressions with assembly-style instructions. It was part of the WebAssembly MVP finished in March 2017, and the W3C published WebAssembly 1.0, which defines the text format, as a Recommendation in December 2019.
WebAssembly Text.releasedEvent: WebAssembly MVP design (including the text format) declared finished, ending the browser preview

Whitespace.creator: Edwin Brady, Chris Morris
Whitespace.history: Whitespace was created by Edwin Brady and Chris Morris at the University of Durham and released on April Fool's Day 2003. It ignores every character except spaces, tabs and newlines, which encode stack, heap and arithmetic operations, so programs can hide in the whitespace of other source code. Brady later created Idris.
Whitespace.releasedEvent: Publicly released, featured on Slashdot on April Fool's Day 2003

Wolfram Language.creator: Stephen Wolfram (Wolfram Research)
Wolfram Language.history: The Wolfram Language is the language of Mathematica, which Stephen Wolfram launched in 1988. It went unnamed for decades because, Wolfram wrote, nobody could agree on a name, and in 2013 it was officially named the Wolfram Language. It is built on symbolic expressions and pattern-based rules, with large built-in libraries of mathematics and curated data.
Wolfram Language.releasedEvent: Mathematica 1.0 launched; the language was named the Wolfram Language in 2013

XQuery.creator: W3C XML Query Working Group
XQuery.history: XQuery 1.0 became a W3C Recommendation in January 2007, edited by a group including Don Chamberlin, a co-designer of SQL. It is a declarative, functional language for searching, extracting and transforming XML data, often described as SQL for XML. Version 3.1 (2017) added maps, arrays and JSON support.
XQuery.releasedEvent: XQuery 1.0 published as a W3C Recommendation

YAML.creator: Clark Evans, Ingy döt Net, Oren Ben-Kiki
YAML.history: YAML was first proposed by Clark Evans in May 2001 and designed with Ingy döt Net and Oren Ben-Kiki, drawing on Ingy's Perl module Data::Denter. The name first stood for Yet Another Markup Language and was later recast as YAML Ain't Markup Language. It is widely used for configuration files, CI pipelines and deployment manifests.
YAML.releasedEvent: Clark Evans posted 'YAML Draft 0.1' to the sml-dev mailing list

Zig.creator: Andrew Kelley
Zig.history: Andrew Kelley started Zig in 2015 as a side project while building a digital audio workstation, aiming for a language more pragmatic than C. It has no hidden control flow, no hidden memory allocations, no preprocessor and no macros, and it can import C headers and compile C code directly.
Zig.releasedEvent: Andrew Kelley's blog post "Introduction to the Zig Programming Language" announcing the language (first repository commit 2015-08-05)

Ada (Script).creator: Jean Ichbiah (CII Honeywell Bull)
Ada (Script).history: The US Department of Defense ran a design competition in the late 1970s to replace the hundreds of languages in its systems; Jean Ichbiah's 'Green' proposal won in May 1979. Named after Ada Lovelace, its standard was approved on her birthday and numbered 1815 for her birth year. It is used in avionics, rail and defense software.
Ada (Script).releasedEvent: MIL-STD-1815 reference manual approved by the US Department of Defense

Assembly (ARM).creator: Sophie Wilson and Steve Furber (Acorn Computers)
Assembly (ARM).history: ARM began at Acorn Computers in 1983 as a small RISC processor for its next computers: Sophie Wilson designed the instruction set and Steve Furber the architecture, first modelled in BBC BASIC. The first ARM1 chips powered up on 26 April 1985 and printed "Hello World, I am ARM". ARM cores now run most phones and many embedded devices.
Assembly (ARM).releasedEvent: First ARM1 processors powered up at Acorn Computers

Assembly (x64).creator: AMD
Assembly (x64).history: x64, also called x86-64 or AMD64, is AMD's 64-bit extension of the x86 instruction set, which it announced in 1999 and specified in 2000. The first processor to implement it, the Opteron, was announced in April 2003, and Intel later adopted the same instruction set. It is the main architecture of desktop PCs and servers.
Assembly (x64).releasedEvent: AMD Opteron, the first AMD64 (x86-64) processor, announced

C (Script).creator: Dennis Ritchie (Bell Labs)
C (Script).history: Dennis Ritchie developed C at Bell Labs from Ken Thompson's B so Unix could be written in a higher-level language; the Version 4 Unix kernel of 1973 was largely rewritten in it. Kernighan and Ritchie's 1978 book defined 'K&R C'. Its syntax shaped C++, Java, C# and many later languages.
C (Script).releasedEvent: Ritchie's new compiler and the language renamed C at Bell Labs

C# Script.creator: Glenn Block (scriptcs); Microsoft Roslyn team (C# Interactive)
C# Script.history: C# scripts (.csx files) let top-level C# statements run without a project, class or Main method. Glenn Block started scriptcs as a side project in 2013 on top of the Roslyn compiler, inspired by Node.js's 'no projects, just script'. Microsoft followed with C# Interactive and csi.exe in Visual Studio 2015 Update 1.
C# Script.releasedEvent: scriptcs, the first runner for .csx C# scripts, launched on Roslyn (InfoQ report 2013-04-25)

C++ (Script).creator: Bjarne Stroustrup (Bell Labs)
C++ (Script).history: Bjarne Stroustrup began 'C with Classes' at Bell Labs in 1979 to add Simula-style classes to C without losing its speed. Rick Mascitti suggested the name C++, first used in December 1983. It was standardized in 1998 and is used for operating systems, browsers, game engines and high-performance software.
C++ (Script).releasedEvent: First commercial release (Cfront Release 1.0) and publication of The C++ Programming Language

Caché MUMPS.creator: InterSystems
Caché MUMPS.history: InterSystems was founded in 1979 to sell MUMPS hierarchical databases. In 1997 it launched Caché as its flagship product and stopped developing its older MUMPS line. Because Caché is at its core a MUMPS implementation, it runs ANSI-standard MUMPS routines unchanged.
Caché MUMPS.releasedEvent: InterSystems launched Caché, which runs ANSI MUMPS routines unchanged

Caché ObjectScript.creator: InterSystems
Caché ObjectScript.history: Caché ObjectScript is a functional superset of ANSI-standard MUMPS that adds classes and objects. InterSystems introduced it with the Caché database in 1997, after combining several MUMPS products. It remains the main language of InterSystems IRIS, used widely in healthcare systems.
Caché ObjectScript.releasedEvent: InterSystems launched Caché with ObjectScript as its main language

Caché ObjectScript (Class).creator: InterSystems
Caché ObjectScript (Class).history: Caché ObjectScript is a functional superset of ANSI-standard MUMPS that adds classes and objects. InterSystems introduced it with the Caché database in 1997, after combining several MUMPS products. It remains the main language of InterSystems IRIS, used widely in healthcare systems.
Caché ObjectScript (Class).releasedEvent: InterSystems launched Caché with ObjectScript as its main language

ClojureScript.creator: Rich Hickey
ClojureScript.history: Rich Hickey announced ClojureScript in 2011 to bring Clojure to browsers and other JavaScript hosts. The compiler emits JavaScript that follows Google Closure conventions and runs the Closure compiler to produce compact, optimized output. It also uses the Closure library for DOM and event handling.
ClojureScript.releasedEvent: Announced by Rich Hickey at the NYC Clojure Group meeting; clojure.org post on 2011-07-22

ClojureScript (Browser).creator: Rich Hickey
ClojureScript (Browser).history: Rich Hickey announced ClojureScript in 2011 to bring Clojure to browsers and other JavaScript hosts. The compiler emits JavaScript that follows Google Closure conventions and runs the Closure compiler to produce compact, optimized output. It also uses the Closure library for DOM and event handling.
ClojureScript (Browser).releasedEvent: Announced by Rich Hickey at the NYC Clojure Group meeting; clojure.org post on 2011-07-22

ClojureScript (Node).creator: Rich Hickey
ClojureScript (Node).history: Rich Hickey announced ClojureScript in 2011 to bring Clojure to browsers and other JavaScript hosts. The compiler emits JavaScript that follows Google Closure conventions and runs the Closure compiler to produce compact, optimized output. It also uses the Closure library for DOM and event handling.
ClojureScript (Node).releasedEvent: Announced by Rich Hickey at the NYC Clojure Group meeting; clojure.org post on 2011-07-22

COBOL (GnuCOBOL).creator: CODASYL Short-Range Committee (Jean Sammet, Howard Bromberg, Vernon Reeves, William Selden, Gertrude Tierney and others); Grace Hopper as technical adviser
COBOL (GnuCOBOL).history: COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language) came out of a May 1959 Pentagon meeting that formed CODASYL to create a common business language. It drew heavily on Grace Hopper's FLOW-MATIC, and in December 1960 the same program ran on RCA and Univac machines. It still runs much of the world's banking and government record keeping.
COBOL (GnuCOBOL).releasedEvent: CODASYL executive committee approved the COBOL 60 specification (printed April 1960)

CoffeeScript (Literate).creator: Jeremy Ashkenas
CoffeeScript (Literate).history: Jeremy Ashkenas released CoffeeScript in December 2009 as a small language that compiles one-to-one into JavaScript, with syntax borrowed from Ruby, Python and Haskell. Arrow functions, classes and destructuring in ES2015 owe much to it.

ColdFusion Script.creator: Allaire Corporation (Jeremy Allaire and J. J. Allaire)
ColdFusion Script.history: CFScript is the JavaScript-like script syntax of CFML, added in ColdFusion 4.0 in 1998 as an alternative to writing logic in tags. Later versions added script functions (ColdFusion 5), try/catch (MX) and full script-based components, so whole applications can now be written without tags.
ColdFusion Script.releasedEvent: Allaire ColdFusion 4.0 released, adding the cfscript tag

Common Lisp (CLISP).creator: Guy L. Steele Jr., Scott Fahlman, Richard P. Gabriel, David A. Moon, Daniel Weinreb, Kent Pitman and others
Common Lisp (CLISP).history: Common Lisp began in 1981 when ARPA manager Bob Engelmore pushed for a single Lisp to unify MacLisp successors. Guy Steele's book Common Lisp the Language (1984) served as its de facto standard until ANSI published the standard in 1994. It includes the Common Lisp Object System (CLOS) and first-class macros.
Common Lisp (CLISP).releasedEvent: Publication of Common Lisp the Language (first edition) by Guy L. Steele Jr.

Common Lisp (SBCL).creator: Guy L. Steele Jr., Scott Fahlman, Richard P. Gabriel, David A. Moon, Daniel Weinreb, Kent Pitman and others
Common Lisp (SBCL).history: Common Lisp began in 1981 when ARPA manager Bob Engelmore pushed for a single Lisp to unify MacLisp successors. Guy Steele's book Common Lisp the Language (1984) served as its de facto standard until ANSI published the standard in 1994. It includes the Common Lisp Object System (CLOS) and first-class macros.
Common Lisp (SBCL).releasedEvent: Publication of Common Lisp the Language (first edition) by Guy L. Steele Jr.

Component Pascal (BlackBox).creator: Oberon microsystems
Component Pascal (BlackBox).history: Component Pascal, first called Oberon/L, is a refinement of Oberon-2 by the ETH Zurich spin-off Oberon microsystems. It ships with the BlackBox Component Builder, which went open source in 2004 and is now maintained by volunteers. Gardens Point Component Pascal from QUT targets .NET and the JVM.
Component Pascal (BlackBox).releasedEvent: Component Pascal (originally Oberon/L) first appeared with Oberon microsystems' BlackBox Component Builder

Erlang (Script).creator: Joe Armstrong, Robert Virding, Mike Williams (Ericsson)
Erlang (Script).history: Erlang was developed at the Ericsson Computer Science Laboratory to program telephone switches, first as an interpreter written in Prolog that proved too slow for products. It was built for massive concurrency, fault tolerance and hot code loading, and the AXD301 switch held over a million lines of it. Ericsson released Erlang/OTP as open source in December 1998.
Erlang (Script).releasedEvent: First Prolog-based implementation at the Ericsson Computer Science Laboratory

F# (Script).creator: Don Syme (Microsoft Research)
F# (Script).history: Don Syme at Microsoft Research Cambridge built F# as an implementation of the core of OCaml for .NET, first released quietly in 2002; a pre-release of F# 1.0 followed in January 2005. It brought type inference, pattern matching and algebraic data types to .NET, shipped in Visual Studio 2010, and was open sourced in 2010.
F# (Script).releasedEvent: F# v0.1 released near-silently on Microsoft Research's site as part of the ILX project

Fortran (Fixed).creator: John Backus (IBM)
Fortran (Fixed).history: John Backus proposed Fortran (Formula Translation) to IBM in late 1953, and his team delivered the first compiler for the IBM 704 in April 1957 after a reference manual in October 1956. As the first widely used high-level language it showed that compiled code could rival hand-written assembly, and it remains central to scientific and numerical computing.
Fortran (Fixed).releasedEvent: First FORTRAN compiler delivered for the IBM 704

Go (Script).creator: Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike, Ken Thompson (Google)
Go (Script).history: Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike and Ken Thompson began sketching Go on a whiteboard at Google on 21 September 2007, frustrated that no mainstream language offered fast compilation, fast execution and ease of programming together. Google open-sourced it on 10 November 2009. It has a small syntax, fast builds and goroutines with channels for concurrency.
Go (Script).releasedEvent: Go announced and open-sourced by Google

Haskell (Literate).creator: Haskell Committee (report editors Paul Hudak and Philip Wadler)
Haskell (Literate).history: A committee formed at the FPCA '87 conference to define one open standard for lazy, purely functional languages, and the Haskell 1.0 Report, edited by Paul Hudak and Philip Wadler, appeared on 1 April 1990. Named after logician Haskell Curry, it has lazy evaluation, static typing and type classes.

Kotlin (Script).creator: JetBrains (lead designer Andrey Breslav)
Kotlin (Script).history: JetBrains unveiled Kotlin in July 2011 as a concise, null-safe language fully interoperable with Java, named after Kotlin Island near Saint Petersburg. Version 1.0 shipped in 2016. Google added official Android support in 2017 and declared Kotlin its preferred language for Android development in 2019.
Kotlin (Script).releasedEvent: JetBrains unveils Project Kotlin (at the JVM Language Summit); Kotlin 1.0 released 2016-02-15

Perl 5 (Script).creator: Larry Wall
Perl 5 (Script).history: Perl 5.000 was a near-complete rewrite of Larry Wall's 1987 interpreter, adding objects, references, lexical variables and modules. CPAN opened in 1995 and Perl 5 became the glue language of the early web. A planned redesign, Perl 6, became the separate language Raku in 2019, and Perl 5 continues to receive yearly releases.

PHP (Script).creator: Rasmus Lerdorf
PHP (Script).history: Rasmus Lerdorf wrote Personal Home Page Tools in 1994 as C CGI binaries to track visits to his online resume, and released the source in June 1995. It became PHP/FI, and the 1998 rewrite by Andi Gutmans and Zeev Suraski, PHP 3, renamed it the recursive PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor. It became one of the most widely used server-side web languages.
PHP (Script).releasedEvent: Rasmus Lerdorf publicly released the source of Personal Home Page Tools

Ruby (Script).creator: Yukihiro Matsumoto
Ruby (Script).history: Yukihiro 'Matz' Matsumoto created Ruby in Japan, naming it in an online chat in February 1993, and blended ideas from Perl, Smalltalk, Eiffel, Ada and Lisp. He aimed to make programmers happy and the language 'natural, not simple'. Ruby on Rails made it a staple of web development in the 2000s.
Ruby (Script).releasedEvent: Ruby 0.95 announced on Japanese domestic newsgroups

Scheme (Script).creator: Guy L. Steele Jr. and Gerald Jay Sussman (MIT AI Lab)
Scheme (Script).history: Gerald Jay Sussman and Guy L. Steele Jr. created Scheme at the MIT AI Lab in 1975 and described it in a series of memos now known as the Lambda Papers. As a minimalist Lisp dialect, it pioneered lexical scoping, block structure and first-class continuations, influencing compiler theory.
Scheme (Script).releasedEvent: MIT AI Memo 349, "SCHEME: An Interpreter for Extended Lambda Calculus", published

Swift (Script).creator: Chris Lattner (Apple)
Swift (Script).history: Chris Lattner started Swift in secret in July 2010, and it became a major focus of Apple's developer tools group in 2013. Apple unveiled it at WWDC in June 2014 as a safer, faster successor to Objective-C for iOS and OS X apps, and open-sourced it in December 2015.
Swift (Script).releasedEvent: Swift announced at Apple's WWDC 2014 keynote, with a beta for developers

Objective-C++.creator: NeXT
Objective-C++.history: Objective-C++ lets one source file mix C++ and Objective-C. NeXT developed it in 1989 at the request of Lotus Development, which was writing the Improv spreadsheet for NeXTSTEP. The GCC and Clang front ends accept it, though the two object models stay separate, so a C++ class cannot inherit from an Objective-C class.
Objective-C++.releasedEvent: Developed at NeXT for Lotus Development's Improv

Gleam.creator: Louis Pilfold
Gleam.history: Louis Pilfold began Gleam in 2016 and released v0.1 in April 2019; version 1.0 followed in March 2024. It is a statically typed functional language that compiles to Erlang for the BEAM VM and to JavaScript, aiming for Erlang's fault tolerance with friendly compiler errors.

Mojo.creator: Chris Lattner and Modular Inc.
Mojo.history: Mojo was announced by Modular, co-founded by LLVM and Swift creator Chris Lattner and Tim Davis, in May 2023. It uses Python syntax and builds on MLIR to give systems-level performance and direct hardware access for AI work. Mojo 1.0 was released in August 2026, and the compiler was open-sourced a week later.
Mojo.releasedEvent: Mojo announced at Modular's launch keynote with an early-access online playground

Solidity.creator: Gavin Wood; developed by Christian Reitwiessner and the Ethereum Solidity team
Solidity.history: Gavin Wood proposed Solidity in 2014 as a contract language for Ethereum, and Christian Reitwiessner began implementing it that October, later leading the Solidity team. It is a statically typed, curly-brace language influenced by C++, Python and JavaScript, and compiles to bytecode for the Ethereum Virtual Machine.
Solidity.releasedEvent: Solidity proposed by Gavin Wood; first implementation commit (scanner) by Christian Reitwiessner on 2014-10-06

Q#.creator: Microsoft Research (Quantum Architectures and Computation group)
Q#.history: Q# was announced at Microsoft Ignite in September 2017 and shipped that December in the Quantum Development Kit, built by Microsoft Research's QuArC group under Krysta Svore. It expresses quantum algorithms with native types for qubits and operations, called from classical host code; the compilers and simulators were open-sourced in 2019.
Q#.releasedEvent: Released in the preview of the Microsoft Quantum Development Kit (announced at Ignite on 2017-09-26)

Befunge.creator: Chris Pressey
Befunge.history: Befunge is a two-dimensional esoteric language created by Chris Pressey in 1993, with the goal of being as hard to compile as possible. The instruction pointer moves up, down, left or right across a grid of single-character commands. It led to Befunge-98 and the Funge family.
Befunge.releasedEvent: Befunge-93 created and released by Chris Pressey

Rockstar.creator: Dylan Beattie
Rockstar.history: Rockstar was created by Dylan Beattie after Paul Stovell tweeted on 3 July 2018 that someone should make a language called Rockstar to confuse recruiters. It satirises 'rockstar developer' job ads by making programs look like lyrics from 1980s hard rock and power ballads, with poetic variable declarations.
Rockstar.releasedEvent: Initial commit of the Rockstar specification repository by Dylan Beattie

Chef.creator: David Morgan-Mar
Chef.history: David Morgan-Mar designed Chef so that programs read like cooking recipes: variables are ingredients, stacks are mixing bowls and output is served in baking dishes. The specification asks that recipes be easy to prepare and delicious. Mike Worth wrote a Hello World that also works as a chocolate cake recipe, and baked it.
Chef.releasedEvent: Published on David Morgan-Mar's esoteric languages site

ArnoldC.creator: Lauri Hartikka
ArnoldC.history: ArnoldC is an esoteric language by Lauri Hartikka whose keywords are Arnold Schwarzenegger movie quotes, such as IT'S SHOWTIME to start a program and TALK TO THE HAND to print. It is written in Scala and compiles to Java bytecode, and it went viral in 2014.
ArnoldC.releasedEvent: ArnoldC repository created on GitHub (first commit)

Odin.creator: Ginger Bill (Bill Hall)
Odin.history: Ginger Bill started Odin one evening in late July 2016 after growing frustrated with C++, wanting C with slices, defer, better variadics and runtime type information. It is a data-oriented systems language with manual memory management and fast compilation. JangaFX writes its EmberGen fluid simulation software in Odin.
Odin.releasedEvent: Development started (per official FAQ); GitHub repository created 2016-11

Nix.creator: Eelco Dolstra (Utrecht University)
Nix.history: Nix came out of Eelco Dolstra's research at Utrecht University, described in his 2006 PhD thesis The Purely Functional Software Deployment Model. Its lazily evaluated, purely functional language describes packages whose builds are isolated and stored by hash. It drives the Nix package manager and the NixOS distribution, presented at ICFP 2008.
Nix.releasedEvent: Initial development and release of Nix (first commit 12 Mar 2003)

Fish.creator: Axel Liljencrantz
Fish.history: The friendly interactive shell (fish) was released by Axel Liljencrantz in 2005. It favors sane defaults, autosuggestions and syntax highlighting over POSIX compatibility. Originally written in C, then C++, it was rewritten in Rust for version 4.0 in 2025.

Zsh.creator: Paul Falstad
Zsh.history: Paul Falstad wrote zsh in 1990 as a Princeton student and posted it to alt.sources as a ksh/tcsh-like shell. The name comes from the login name of teaching assistant Zhong Shao. It extends the Bourne shell with programmable completion and extended globbing, and became the default login shell in macOS Catalina in 2019.
Zsh.releasedEvent: zsh 1.0 posted to alt.sources in 8 parts by Paul Falstad

Emacs Lisp.creator: Richard Stallman, Guy L. Steele Jr.
Emacs Lisp.history: Emacs Lisp is the Lisp dialect built into GNU Emacs, which Richard Stallman developed from Gosling Emacs and gave a real Lisp as its extension language. It is mainly inspired by Maclisp, with some Common Lisp influence, and was kept small to save memory. Most of Emacs itself is written in it, and users can redefine almost any part of the editor at runtime.
Emacs Lisp.releasedEvent: GNU Emacs 13, the initial public release, announced on Usenet

GDScript.creator: Juan Linietsky, Ariel Manzur
GDScript.history: GDScript was built by Juan Linietsky and Ariel Manzur for Godot, an in-house engine they opened to the public under the MIT license in January 2014. After trying Python, Lua and Squirrel, they wrote their own language for tighter editor integration. Its indentation-based syntax is tuned for scene and node scripting.
GDScript.releasedEvent: First public, open-source release of the Godot engine

PureScript.creator: Phil Freeman
PureScript.history: PureScript is a Haskell-inspired language that compiles to readable JavaScript. Phil Freeman started it in 2013 because he was dissatisfied with existing Haskell-to-JavaScript tools such as Fay, Haste and GHCJS; the community later built its build tool Pulp, the Pursuit documentation site and the Spago package manager.
PureScript.releasedEvent: Initial commit of the PureScript compiler repository by Phil Freeman (no announcement found)

Idris.creator: Edwin Brady (University of St Andrews)
Idris.history: Edwin Brady designed Idris at the University of St Andrews as a general-purpose language with dependent types, in which types are first-class values and programs can be checked against precise specifications at compile time. Idris 2, a self-hosted rewrite based on quantitative type theory, compiles to Scheme and C.
Idris.releasedEvent: Earliest archived Idris project page at the University of St Andrews

Lean.creator: Leonardo de Moura (Microsoft Research)
Lean.history: Lean is a theorem prover and programming language started by Leonardo de Moura at Microsoft Research in 2013. Lean 4, a reimplementation written mostly in Lean itself, appeared in 2021. Its community library mathlib formalizes a large part of modern mathematics, and the Lean FRO nonprofit has supported development since 2023.
Lean.releasedEvent: First commit in the leanprover/lean repository (no announcement found; the system paper appeared at CADE 2015)

Agda.creator: Ulf Norell (Chalmers University of Technology); original Agda by Catarina Coquand
Agda.history: Agda is a dependently typed functional language and proof assistant from Chalmers University. Catarina Coquand wrote the original system in 1999, and Ulf Norell's Agda 2 rewrite is the current language. The name comes from a Swedish song about a hen called Agda, a nod to the Coq proof assistant.
Agda.releasedEvent: Agda 2, a full rewrite by Ulf Norell described in his PhD thesis

Pony.creator: Sylvan Clebsch
Pony.history: Sylvan Clebsch began designing Pony after his C actor library for trading systems kept hitting data races, and in 2014 co-founded Causality to build the compiler. Reference capabilities in the type system rule out data races without locks, and each actor has its own garbage collector. The name came from a friend's reply to his plans: "yeah, and I want a pony."

Red.creator: Nenad Rakocevic
Red.history: Red was announced by Nenad Rakocevic, a long-time Rebol developer, in 2011 as a successor to Rebol with similar syntax and semantics. It ships a small compiler toolchain and a low-level Red/System dialect used to implement itself, and Red/System was the first part to be released.
Red.releasedEvent: Announced at the ReBorCon 2011 conference in the Netherlands

Hy.creator: Paul Tagliamonte
Hy.history: Paul Tagliamonte started Hy in December 2012 as a Lisp dialect that compiles to Python's abstract syntax tree, and introduced it with a lightning talk at PyCon 2013. It gives full access to Python libraries from s-expression syntax, and Python code can import Hy modules in turn.

Fennel.creator: Calvin Rose
Fennel.history: Fennel is a Lisp that compiles to Lua, started by Calvin Rose in 2016 as a test bed for Lisp ideas on top of Lua. It adds macros and pattern matching with no runtime overhead, and its output runs anywhere Lua does, including game frameworks such as LÖVE and TIC-80.
Fennel.releasedEvent: First commit in the public GitHub repository

Janet.creator: Calvin Rose
Janet.history: Janet is a small embeddable Lisp-like language by Calvin Rose, who earlier created Fennel on top of Lua. Janet is written from scratch in C and ships as a single binary with a bytecode VM, a built-in PEG library, green threads and an event loop. It embeds in C programs with just janet.c and janet.h.
Janet.releasedEvent: Development began in public on GitHub (first commit 2017-02-09, repo created 2017-03-10); first tagged release 0.1.0 on 2018-12-09

Vala.creator: Jürg Billeter and Raffaele Sandrini
Vala.history: Vala is an object-oriented language for the GObject type system, conceived by Jürg Billeter and implemented with Raffaele Sandrini in 2006. It compiles to C, so programs need no extra runtime, and it is used for GNOME and elementary OS applications. The compiler became self-hosting with version 0.1.0 in 2007.

ReScript.creator: Hongbo Zhang and the ReScript team (from Bloomberg's BuckleScript)
ReScript.history: ReScript grew from BuckleScript, an OCaml-to-JavaScript compiler that Hongbo Zhang released at Bloomberg in 2016 and that served as Reason's JavaScript backend. In 2020 the team gave it its own syntax and renamed it, focusing on the JavaScript ecosystem with an OCaml-style type system and fast compilation to readable JavaScript.
ReScript.releasedEvent: BuckleScript rebranded as ReScript (official blog announcement)

Nushell.creator: Sophia Turner, Yehuda Katz, Andrés Robalino
Nushell.history: Nushell was announced in August 2019 after Yehuda Katz, impressed by PowerShell, pitched the idea of a structured shell to Sophia Turner. Commands pass tables of data instead of raw text, so pipelines filter and sort like queries. It is written in Rust, runs on Windows, Linux and macOS, and borrows Rust-style error messages.

Wren.creator: Bob Nystrom
Wren.history: Wren is a small class-based scripting language by Bob Nystrom, a former game developer who found Lua's approach to objects awkward. It is made to be embedded in applications, its VM is under 4,000 semicolons of C, and it uses fibers for concurrency. Nystrom later wrote the book Crafting Interpreters.

Squirrel.creator: Alberto Demichelis
Squirrel.history: Alberto Demichelis announced Squirrel in September 2003 as a scripting language for games with tight size, memory and real-time limits; its compiler and VM fit in about 6,000 lines of C++. Valve uses it for VScripts in Left 4 Dead 2 and Portal 2, and OpenTTD embeds it.
Squirrel.releasedEvent: Alberto Demichelis's announcement "[ANN] Squirrel yet another scripting language" posted to comp.compilers

MoonScript.creator: Leaf Corcoran
MoonScript.history: MoonScript is a language by Leaf Corcoran that compiles to Lua, inspired by CoffeeScript. It adds indentation-based syntax, classes and comprehensions, and runs anywhere Lua does. Corcoran also created the itch.io platform and the Lapis web framework, both of which use it.
MoonScript.releasedEvent: MoonScript v0.1.0 tagged in the official repository (first commit 16 May 2011)

BQN.creator: Marshall Lochbaum
BQN.history: Marshall Lochbaum began BQN as a 'fixed APL' while working at Dyalog and made it a personal project after leaving in early 2020.
