It drops compatibility with APL and J to clean up syntax and semantics and has a formal specification. The name comes from shifting each letter of 'APL' forward by one.
BQN.releasedEvent: BQN published by Marshall Lochbaum after leaving Dyalog (repository first commit 2020-06-05)

Jsonnet.creator: Dave Cunningham (Google)
Jsonnet.history: Jsonnet began in early 2014 as a 20% project by Dave Cunningham at Google. It extends JSON with variables, functions, imports and inheritance, and any valid JSON file is also a valid Jsonnet program. The name joins JSON and sonnet.
Jsonnet.releasedEvent: Open-source launch on GitHub (first commit; Google Open Source Blog introduced it on 2015-04-20)

Pike.creator: Fredrik Hübinette
Pike.history: Pike descends from LPC, Lars Pensjö's language for multiplayer adventure games. In 1994 Fredrik Hübinette wrote a new GPL interpreter, µLPC, which InformationsVävarna adopted for its web server, and in 1996 it was renamed Pike. It powered the Roxen web server, and Linköping University has maintained it since 2002.
Pike.releasedEvent: µLPC, Pike's predecessor, begun and released under the GPL

Hare.creator: Drew DeVault
Hare.history: Drew DeVault and contributors developed Hare privately for about two and a half years before announcing it in April 2022. It is a small systems language close to C, with manual memory management, a minimal runtime and the QBE compiler backend, and its programs do not link to libc by default.

Carbon.creator: Chandler Carruth (Google)
Carbon.history: Chandler Carruth introduced Carbon at CppNorth in 2022 as an experimental successor to C++. Its main goals are readable syntax and bidirectional interoperability with existing C++ code. It is developed in the open on GitHub and has not yet reached a 1.0 release.
Carbon.releasedEvent: Announced by Chandler Carruth in a CppNorth keynote in Toronto

Uiua.creator: Kai Schmidt
Uiua.history: Uiua is a stack-based array language by Kai Schmidt. It combines APL-style array operations with Forth-like stack manipulation and writes primitives as Unicode glyphs, mostly inspired by BQN. Its online pad and step-through examples drew wide attention when it reached the top of Hacker News in September 2023.
Uiua.releasedEvent: First public attention: changelog begins 2023-09-28 and the Hacker News launch thread (with the author commenting) was posted 2023-09-27

V.creator: Alexander Medvednikov
V.history: V (Vlang) is a statically typed compiled language by Alexander Medvednikov, who first wrote it for his Volt desktop messenger. Its open-source release in June 2019 drew wide attention, and it emphasizes fast compilation, no global state and easy C interop.
V.releasedEvent: V 0.0.12 open-source release committed to the public GitHub repository

Ook!.creator: David Morgan-Mar
Ook!.history: David Morgan-Mar created Ook! as a language designed for orangutans. It is a one-to-one encoding of Brainfuck using pairs of the tokens Ook., Ook? and Ook!, so it is Turing-complete.
Ook!.releasedEvent: Published on David Morgan-Mar's esoteric languages site

Standard ML.creator: Robin Milner, Mads Tofte, Robert Harper and David MacQueen
Standard ML.history: Standard ML grew out of the ML metalanguage that Robin Milner built for the LCF prover in the 1970s; in 1983 he drafted a proposal to unify ML's dialects. The Definition of Standard ML (1990, revised 1997) specifies the language and its type system formally.
Standard ML.releasedEvent: First draft of Robin Milner's "A Proposal for Standard ML" discussed at the first Standard ML meeting in Edinburgh

Modula-3.creator: Luca Cardelli, James Donahue, Lucille Glassman, Mick Jordan, Bill Kalsow, Greg Nelson (DEC SRC and Olivetti)
Modula-3.history: Modula-3 began in November 1986 when Maurice Wilkes wrote to Niklaus Wirth proposing a new Modula, and was designed at DEC Systems Research Center and Olivetti as a safer successor to Modula-2 and Modula-2+. It added objects, threads, exceptions and garbage collection, and was popular for teaching in the 1990s.
Modula-3.releasedEvent: Modula-3 language definition completed (revised report published November 1989)

Oberon.creator: Niklaus Wirth (ETH Zurich)
Oberon.history: Niklaus Wirth designed Oberon in 1987 at ETH Zurich as a simplified successor to Modula-2, and wrote the Oberon operating system with Jürg Gutknecht in it. Its main new feature was type extension of records. The name comes from Voyager's images of Uranus's moon Oberon, and later revisions include Oberon-2 (1991) and Oberon-07.
Oberon.releasedEvent: Language first published by Niklaus Wirth at ETH Zurich

PL/I.creator: IBM and the SHARE user group
PL/I.history: In 1963 IBM and SHARE formed a committee to extend Fortran, and it produced a new ALGOL-like language first defined in 1964 as NPL, renamed PL/I in 1965. It aimed to combine scientific and business programming in one language. Multics was written largely in a subset, Early PL/I.
PL/I.releasedEvent: First compiler, PL/I F Release 1 for OS/360, shipped (first definition as NPL in April 1964)

SNOBOL.creator: David J. Farber, Ralph E. Griswold and Ivan P. Polonsky (Bell Labs)
SNOBOL.history: David Farber, Ralph Griswold and Ivan Polonsky created SNOBOL at Bell Labs and described it in the Journal of the ACM in January 1964. The team reportedly considered the name SEXI before settling on SNOBOL. Its string pattern matching, refined through SNOBOL4 (1967), inspired later text tools and Griswold's Icon language.
SNOBOL.releasedEvent: First SNOBOL implementation at Bell Labs (published in the Journal of the ACM, January 1964)

Dhall.creator: Gabriella Gonzalez
Dhall.history: Gabriella Gonzalez created Dhall to answer objections to programmable configuration files, most of which come down to Turing completeness. Dhall adds functions, types and imports to JSON-like data but is strongly normalising, so evaluation always terminates. It converts to JSON and YAML.
Dhall.releasedEvent: Gabriella Gonzalez announced Dhall on the Haskell for all blog

CUDA.creator: NVIDIA (Ian Buck, John Nickolls)
CUDA.history: CUDA grew out of Ian Buck's Brook GPU language at Stanford; NVIDIA hired him in 2004 and, with John Nickolls, turned it into CUDA. It extends C and C++ with kernels that run across thousands of GPU threads, and it now underpins most deep learning frameworks.

Vyper.creator: Vitalik Buterin
Vyper.history: Vyper is a Python-like language for Ethereum smart contracts, started by Vitalik Buterin in November 2016 under the name Viper as a simpler, more auditable alternative to Solidity. It deliberately leaves out features such as inheritance and operator overloading to make audits easier.
Vyper.releasedEvent: First commit by Vitalik Buterin in the public repository (then named Viper); first beta 0.1.0b1 on PyPI in 2018

LaTeX.creator: Leslie Lamport (SRI International)
LaTeX.history: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX at SRI International in the early 1980s as a macro package on top of Donald Knuth's TeX, so authors could describe structure rather than layout. His 1986 manual sold hundreds of thousands of copies. Frank Mittelbach's team took over in 1989 and released LaTeX2e in 1994, still the standard for scientific publishing.
LaTeX.releasedEvent: First versions of Lamport's LaTeX macros released

PostScript.creator: John Warnock, Chuck Geschke, Doug Brotz, Ed Taft, Bill Paxton (Adobe)
PostScript.history: John Warnock and Chuck Geschke left Xerox PARC, where they had worked on Interpress, and founded Adobe in December 1982 to build a simpler page description language. PostScript is a stack-based language like Forth, and the Apple LaserWriter of 1985 was the first printer to ship with it, starting desktop publishing.

CMake.creator: Bill Hoffman, Ken Martin, Brad King and others (Kitware)
CMake.history: Kitware began CMake in 1999, with National Library of Medicine funding, to build the Insight Segmentation and Registration Toolkit (ITK) on many platforms. Its authors wrote their own small scripting language instead of using Tcl. CMake generates native Makefiles and IDE projects and is now the most common build system for C and C++.
CMake.releasedEvent: First release of CMake by Kitware

SystemVerilog.creator: Accellera (based on Superlog from Co-Design Automation and OpenVera from Synopsys)
SystemVerilog.history: SystemVerilog started in 2002 when Co-Design Automation donated its Superlog language to Accellera, which approved SystemVerilog 3.0 that June; Synopsys later donated OpenVera for its verification features. It became IEEE 1800 in 2005 and absorbed the base Verilog standard in 2009.
SystemVerilog.releasedEvent: SystemVerilog 3.0 approved as an Accellera standard

Elvish.creator: Qi Xiao
Elvish.history: Elvish is a shell with a real programming language behind it, written in Go by Qi Xiao from 2013 and first shown publicly at a FOSDEM 2015 lightning talk. Its pipelines can carry structured values such as lists and maps instead of plain text, and it has namespaces, closures and exceptions.
Elvish.releasedEvent: First commit ('das, an experimental Unix shell') in the public GitHub repository

Starlark.creator: Google (Bazel team)
Starlark.history: Starlark began as Skylark, the extension language of Google's Blaze build tool, replacing a Python preprocessing step for BUILD files; it shipped with Bazel when Google open-sourced it in 2015 and was renamed Starlark in 2018 for trademark reasons. It is a deterministic, hermetic Python dialect, also used by Buck and Pants.
Starlark.releasedEvent: Skylark (later Starlark) included in the first public source import of Bazel on GitHub

Nelua.creator: Eduardo Bart
Nelua.history: Nelua (Native Extensible Lua) was created by Eduardo Bart in 2019 as a statically typed language with Lua syntax for performance-sensitive work where Lua is too slow. It compiles to C and then to native code, with compile-time metaprogramming written in Lua. It is still in alpha.
Nelua.releasedEvent: First commit in the official repository

Koka.creator: Daan Leijen (Microsoft Research)
Koka.history: Koka is a research language by Daan Leijen at Microsoft Research. Its type system tracks side effects in function types as row-polymorphic, and later algebraic, effects. Koka 2 introduced Perceus, a precise reference counting scheme that lets functional code reuse memory in place.
Koka.releasedEvent: First presented by Daan Leijen at Microsoft Research (2012 overview; earliest repository commit 2012-08-24)

Flix.creator: Magnus Madsen (Aarhus University)
Flix.history: Flix started as a Datalog-inspired language for static program analysis, presented at PLDI 2016 by Magnus Madsen, Ming-Ho Yee and Ondřej Lhoták. It grew into a functional language for the JVM with first-class Datalog constraints and an effect system, developed at Aarhus University with collaborators from Waterloo and other universities.
Flix.releasedEvent: First paper 'From Datalog to Flix' at PLDI 2016 and first GitHub snapshot release (2016-06-09)

Oz.creator: Gert Smolka and students (Saarland University)
Oz.history: Oz was designed in 1991 by Gert Smolka and his students, and from 1996 developed with Seif Haridi and Peter Van Roy at SICS; the Mozart Consortium has maintained it since 1999. It combines logic, functional, object-oriented, constraint and concurrent programming. It is the language of the textbook Concepts, Techniques, and Models of Computer Programming (2004).
Oz.releasedEvent: Language designed by Gert Smolka's group at Saarland University

Nemerle.creator: Kamil Skalski, Michał Moskal, Leszek Pacholski, Paweł Olszta (University of Wrocław)
Nemerle.history: Nemerle was created at the University of Wrocław as a .NET language blending object-oriented and functional styles, with a hygienic macro system. Work began in 2003 and version 0.1 was released as a preview in 2004. JetBrains hired the core developers in 2012 to build the Nitra language framework.
Nemerle.releasedEvent: Nemerle 0.1 announced on the Mono mailing list

Delphi.creator: Anders Hejlsberg (chief architect) and the Borland Delphi team
Delphi.history: Borland launched Delphi on Valentine's Day 1995, with Anders Hejlsberg as chief architect; a stop-ship bug moved the final build to 15 February. It pairs Object Pascal with the Visual Component Library for fast Windows development. Hejlsberg later designed C# and TypeScript at Microsoft.
Delphi.releasedEvent: Delphi 1 launched at the Software Development Conference West in San Francisco

Curry.creator: Michael Hanus, Herbert Kuchen, Juan José Moreno-Navarro
Curry.history: Curry was proposed in 1995 as a standard language for integrated functional logic programming, combining Haskell-style syntax with logic variables and non-deterministic search. It grew into an international initiative coordinated by Michael Hanus at Kiel.
Curry.releasedEvent: Paper 'Curry: A Truly Functional Logic Language' at the ILPS'95 workshop

Pawn.creator: Thiadmer Riemersma (CompuPhase)
Pawn.history: Thiadmer Riemersma began looking in 1997 for a small, fast scripting language he could embed in resource and animation files, and released Small publicly in 1998; it was introduced in Dr. Dobb's Journal in 1999 and later renamed Pawn. It compiles to compact bytecode and runs on microcontrollers as well as desktops and consoles.
Pawn.releasedEvent: First public release, under the name Small

Simula.creator: Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard (Norwegian Computing Center)
Simula.history: Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard built Simula at the Norwegian Computing Center in Oslo, first as the simulation language Simula I (1962 to 1965). Simula 67 introduced classes, objects, inheritance and virtual methods, and influenced Smalltalk and C++. The pair received the 2001 Turing Award for it.
Simula.releasedEvent: Dahl and Nygaard's "Class and Subclass Declarations" presented at the IFIP Working Conference on Simulation Languages, Lysebu, Oslo (first definition of Simula 67)

BCPL.creator: Martin Richards (University of Cambridge)
BCPL.history: Martin Richards designed BCPL in 1966 as a simplified version of CPL and first implemented it at MIT in 1967. Its typeless design led to B and then C. The Jargon File names BCPL as the language of the original Hello World program.
BCPL.releasedEvent: First implementation by Martin Richards at MIT (Project MAC), spring 1967

PicoLisp.creator: Alexander Burger
PicoLisp.history: Alexander Burger's first PicoLisp versions ran in 1988 on a Mac II and were portable to DOS and SCO Unix; it has run mainly on Linux since 1993. The whole system is built on a single data type, the cell, and includes a database with persistent symbols and a browser-based GUI framework. The C version was released under the GPL in 2002.
PicoLisp.releasedEvent: First versions running on a Mac II

newLISP.creator: Lutz Mueller
newLISP.history: Lutz Mueller began newLISP in 1991 on a Sun-4 workstation, moved it to Windows, and released version 1.3 on CompuServe around 1993. It became GPL open source when ported to Linux in 1999. It is a scripting-oriented Lisp that emphasizes small size, built-in networking and string handling.
newLISP.releasedEvent: First version developed on a Sun-4 workstation

Stata.creator: William Gould (Computing Resource Center, now StataCorp)
Stata.history: William Gould began Stata in 1984 at Computing Resource Center in California, and version 1.0 shipped for MS-DOS in January 1985 with 44 commands. The company moved to College Station, Texas, in 1993 and became StataCorp. Scripts are saved as do-files and are common in economics and epidemiology.
Stata.releasedEvent: Stata 1.0 released for MS-DOS with 44 commands

SAS.creator: Anthony Barr and James Goodnight (North Carolina State University)
SAS.history: SAS, the Statistical Analysis System, grew from statistics software Anthony Barr began adapting for IBM System/360 at North Carolina State University in 1966, with James Goodnight writing the statistical routines. Barr, Goodnight, John Sall and Jane Helwig incorporated SAS Institute in 1976. Its data step language processes large tables.
SAS.releasedEvent: Beta (limited) release SAS 71 for IBM mainframes; first full version SAS 72 followed in 1972

Processing.creator: Casey Reas and Ben Fry
Processing.history: Casey Reas and Ben Fry started Processing in 2001 at the MIT Media Lab's Aesthetics and Computation Group, as a successor to John Maeda's Design By Numbers. It wraps Java in a sketchbook to teach programming through visual output, and Daniel Shiffman later joined as a lead.
Processing.releasedEvent: Project begun and first released at the MIT Media Lab

Arduino.creator: Massimo Banzi, David Cuartielles, Tom Igoe, Gianluca Martino, David Mellis (Interaction Design Institute Ivrea)
Arduino.history: Arduino sketches are C++ programs on top of a simple framework. The project forked Hernando Barragán's Wiring platform in 2005 to target cheaper ATmega8 chips, and it is named after the Bar di Re Arduino in Ivrea where the founders met. It made microcontroller programming common in schools and hobby electronics.
Arduino.releasedEvent: Arduino project started at the Interaction Design Institute Ivrea as a fork of Wiring

Cairo.creator: StarkWare (Lior Goldberg, Shahar Papini, Michael Riabzev)
Cairo.history: StarkWare designed Cairo so developers could write programs whose execution is proven with STARK proofs instead of hand-writing polynomial constraints. It began as an assembly-like language, announced in August 2020 and used in production by StarkEx. Cairo 1.0, announced in 2022, is a higher-level rewrite used for Starknet contracts.
Cairo.releasedEvent: StarkWare released the first public Cairo toolchain (version 0.0.1)

Dockerfile.creator: Solomon Hykes and the Docker team (dotCloud)
Dockerfile.history: Solomon Hykes and dotCloud released Docker in March 2013, and the Dockerfile build format followed within weeks. Each instruction such as FROM, RUN or COPY adds a layer to a container image, which made image builds reproducible and scriptable.
Dockerfile.releasedEvent: Docker 0.2.1 changelog lists the first Dockerfile operations (maintainer, expose, cmd)

Makefile.creator: Stuart Feldman (Bell Labs)
Makefile.history: Stuart Feldman wrote make at Bell Labs in April 1976 after Steve Johnson, author of yacc, lost a morning debugging a program whose fix had not been recompiled. Feldman built it over a weekend. Makefiles declare targets and dependencies, and GNU Make is still the default build tool for many C projects.
Makefile.releasedEvent: Early version of make completed at Bell Labs (first shipped in PWB/UNIX 1.0)

Joy.creator: Manfred von Thun (La Trobe University)
Joy.history: Joy is a purely functional concatenative language by Manfred von Thun of La Trobe University in Melbourne. Instead of applying functions to arguments, programs compose functions that act on a stack, and quoted lists serve as programs. It was inspired by Backus's FP and influenced Factor and Cat.
Joy.releasedEvent: First appearance per Wikipedia; 'Joy: Forth's Functional Cousin' presented at EuroForth, 2001-10-09

GolfScript.creator: Darren Smith
GolfScript.history: GolfScript was written by Darren Smith (known as flagitious in Ruby golfing circles) for code golf and released in December 2007; a day later it was added to shinh's golf server. Programs are short stack scripts interpreted by a Ruby program, and the stack is printed when the program ends.

ABAP.creator: SAP SE
ABAP.history: ABAP began as the report language of SAP's R/2 mainframe system; the name originally stood for Allgemeiner Berichts-Aufbereitungs-Prozessor (generic report preparation processor), later read as Advanced Business Application Programming. SAP built R/3 in it, added ABAP Objects around 1999, and it still runs most custom logic in SAP ERP systems.
ABAP.releasedEvent: First appearance as the report language of SAP R/2

ATS.creator: Hongwei Xi (Boston University)
ATS.history: ATS (Applied Type System) was designed by Hongwei Xi at Boston University and absorbed his earlier Dependent ML. It combines dependent and linear types with C-level performance, so programmers can prove memory safety of low-level code at compile time. ATS2 (Postiats) followed in 2013.

bc.creator: Lorinda Cherry and Robert Morris (Bell Labs)
bc.history: bc was written at Bell Labs and appeared in Version 6 Unix. It began as a compiler from a C-like syntax to the dc stack calculator, and its arbitrary-precision arithmetic made it a POSIX standard tool in 1991. GNU bc by Philip A. Nelson is the common modern version.

C3.creator: Christoffer Lernö
C3.history: C3 started as an experimental fork of Bas van den Berg's C2 language, to which Christoffer Lernö had contributed. It keeps C's syntax and ABI compatibility while adding modules, generics, contracts, macros and error handling with optional results. Version 0.5 was the first feature-stable release.
C3.releasedEvent: C3 compiler repository started by Christoffer Lernö (first commit 2019-07-12)

Carp.creator: Erik Svedäng
Carp.history: Erik Svedäng created Carp out of frustration with game-making tools and a love of Lisp. It is a statically typed Lisp with no garbage collector, using inferred types and ownership-based memory management, and compiles to C. The first compiler was written in C in 2015-2016 and rewritten in Haskell in 2017.
Carp.releasedEvent: Carp compiler published on GitHub (first commit 2016-01-11)

ChucK.creator: Ge Wang & Perry Cook (Princeton University)
ChucK.history: Ge Wang created ChucK as a Princeton graduate student with Perry Cook for real-time sound synthesis and live coding. Its 'strongly-timed' model makes time a first-class value that programs advance explicitly. It powered the Princeton and Stanford laptop orchestras and early Smule apps such as Ocarina.
ChucK.releasedEvent: ChucK introduced by Ge Wang and Perry Cook at Princeton

Civet.creator: Daniel X. Moore
Civet.history: Daniel X. Moore started Civet as a CoffeeScript-inspired language that compiles to TypeScript or JavaScript. It keeps about 99% compatibility with existing JS/TS code and adds pipelines, pattern matching, chained comparisons and indentation-based blocks, while TypeScript tooling still type-checks the result.

Coconut.creator: Evan Hubinger
Coconut.history: Evan Hubinger created Coconut as a functional superset of Python: every valid Python 3 program is valid Coconut. It adds pipelines, pattern matching, algebraic data types, partial application and tail call optimisation, and compiles to plain Python that runs on any Python version.

dc.creator: Robert Morris and Lorinda Cherry (Bell Labs)
dc.history: dc (desk calculator) is one of the oldest Unix programs and predates C; it was written in B and was reportedly among the first programs to run on Bell Labs' PDP-11. It is a reverse Polish, arbitrary-precision calculator, and bc was originally built as a front end to it.
dc.releasedEvent: dc(I) desk calculator documented in the First Edition Unix Programmer's Manual

Effekt.creator: Jonathan Immanuel Brachthäuser, Philipp Schuster, Klaus Ostermann (University of Tübingen)
Effekt.history: Effekt was developed at the University of Tübingen to make effect handlers practical. Its 2020 OOPSLA paper 'Effects as Capabilities' tracks what a computation needs from its context instead of what effects it performs, using second-class functions. It compiles to JavaScript, LLVM and other back ends.
Effekt.releasedEvent: First tagged GitHub release (v0.1.6) of the Effekt compiler

Emojicode.creator: Theo Weidmann
Emojicode.history: Theo Weidmann began experimenting with an emoji-based language in 2014 and released Emojicode publicly in January 2016. Despite the joke surface it is a statically typed, object-oriented language with optionals, generics, protocols and closures, compiled to native code through LLVM. Codecademy has offered an Emojicode course since World Emoji Day 2020.
Emojicode.releasedEvent: First public version released on GitHub (per Theo Weidmann)

Euphoria.creator: Robert Craig (Rapid Deployment Software)
Euphoria.history: Robert Craig of Rapid Deployment Software in Toronto first built Euphoria on an Atari ST, but the first public release, version 1.0 in July 1993, was for MS-DOS. Built around a single flexible 'sequence' data type, it was known for being simple and fast for an interpreter. It became open source in 2006 and continues as OpenEuphoria.

F*.creator: Nikhil Swamy, Juan Chen, Cédric Fournet, Pierre-Yves Strub, Karthikeyan Bhargavan, Jean Yang (Microsoft Research, Inria)
F*.history: F* (F star) is a dependently typed functional language from Microsoft Research and Inria for writing programs together with proofs of their correctness. Verified code produced with it is deployed widely: the HACL* cryptography library is used in Firefox's NSS, in Python's hashlib and in WireGuard's Curve25519 code in the Linux kernel.

Fantom.creator: Brian Frank, Andy Frank
Fantom.history: Brothers Brian and Andy Frank began Fan in 2005 to run the same code on the JVM and .NET, later adding JavaScript in browsers. It was renamed Fantom in 2009 because 'Fan' was hard to search for. It mixes static and dynamic typing, and their company SkyFoundry built the SkySpark building-analytics platform in it.
Fantom.releasedEvent: First public release of Fan (renamed Fantom in November 2009)

Grain.creator: Oscar Spencer & Philip Blair
Grain.history: Oscar Spencer and Philip Blair started Grain in 2017 as a side project, after a compilers course and just as browsers enabled WebAssembly by default. It is an ML-family language with type inference and pattern matching whose only compile target is WebAssembly, and its compiler is written in OCaml and ReasonML.

Imba.creator: Sindre Aarsaether
Imba.history: Sindre Aarsaether began Imba around 2011 because he missed Ruby's elegance when writing browser JavaScript, and published it on npm in 2015. It compiles to JavaScript with HTML-like tags and styles built into the syntax. He co-founded Scrimba, the interactive coding-screencast platform built with Imba, whose name blends "scribble" and "Imba".

Inko.creator: Yorick Peterse
Inko.history: Yorick Peterse started Inko in 2015 to make concurrent software easy to write safely, and launched its website and first tagged release in 2018. It uses single ownership with move semantics and lightweight processes that share no memory, and compiles to native code through LLVM.
Inko.releasedEvent: Inko website and manual introduced (first tagged release v0.1.0 followed that month)

INTERCAL.creator: Don Woods & James M. Lyon
INTERCAL.history: INTERCAL (Compiler Language With No Pronounceable Acronym) was invented in 1972 by Don Woods and James Lyon at Princeton as a parody with no similarities to existing languages. It is the original esoteric language, famous for requiring programs to say PLEASE often enough, but not too often. Eric S. Raymond's C-INTERCAL revived it in 1990.

Jakt.creator: Andreas Kling & SerenityOS contributors
Jakt.history: Jakt began in May 2022 as an offshoot of SerenityOS, led by Andreas Kling, to give the project a memory-safe systems language. Its name is Swedish for 'hunt'. It uses automatic reference counting and transpiles to C++, and its first compiler was written in Rust.
Jakt.releasedEvent: First commit in the official SerenityOS/jakt repository (no formal announcement found)

Jasmin.creator: Jonathan Meyer
Jasmin.history: Jasmin was written by Jonathan Meyer as a companion to 'Java Virtual Machine', the O'Reilly book he co-wrote with Troy Downing. Sun had published no assembler format for the JVM, so Jasmin became the de facto way to write class files by hand and a common target for teaching compilers. It lives on as a SourceForge project.
Jasmin.releasedEvent: Jasmin documentation dated July 1996, released as companion to the O'Reilly book 'Java Virtual Machine'

LFE.creator: Robert Virding
LFE.history: LFE (Lisp Flavoured Erlang) was created by Robert Virding, one of the co-creators of Erlang, who began prototyping it in 2007. It is a Lisp with macros that compiles to the Erlang VM and interoperates fully with Erlang and OTP.
LFE.releasedEvent: First release announced by Robert Virding on the erlang-questions mailing list

LLVM IR.creator: Chris Lattner & Vikram Adve (University of Illinois)
LLVM IR.history: LLVM began in 2000 as Chris Lattner's research project under Vikram Adve at the University of Illinois. Its typed SSA intermediate representation became the shared back end of Clang, Rust, Swift, Julia and many other compilers. The name once stood for Low Level Virtual Machine but is no longer an acronym.

Lobster.creator: Wouter van Oortmerssen
Lobster.history: Lobster was created by Wouter van Oortmerssen, also known for FlatBuffers and the Cube engine, who began it around 2010. It is a Python-like language with static type inference and compile-time reference counting, built for game programming, with an OpenGL engine included.
Lobster.releasedEvent: Open-sourced on GitHub (first commit); press coverage of the release followed in June 2013

Luau.creator: Roblox (Arseny Kapoulkine, lead designer)
Luau.history: Roblox had used Lua 5.1 since around 2006 and built Luau from it to get more speed and a type system, after rejecting LuaJIT for poor console support. It shipped as the 'Faster Lua VM' in 2019, gained gradual typing, and was open-sourced under the MIT License on 3 November 2021.
Luau.releasedEvent: New Lua VM ('Faster Lua VM', later named Luau) went live on all Roblox platforms

M4.creator: Brian Kernighan and Dennis Ritchie (Bell Labs)
M4.history: Brian Kernighan and Dennis Ritchie wrote m4 at Bell Labs in 1977 as an extension of Ritchie's earlier m3 macro processor, drawing on ideas from Christopher Strachey. Text without macros passes straight through, which is why a plain line prints itself. GNU Autoconf and sendmail.cf generation still depend on it.
M4.releasedEvent: m4 macro processor written at Bell Labs (shipped with Version 7 Unix)

Motoko.creator: DFINITY Foundation (team led by Andreas Rossberg)
Motoko.history: Motoko was created at the DFINITY Foundation by a team led by Andreas Rossberg, a co-designer of WebAssembly, for writing canister smart contracts on the Internet Computer. Programs are actors with orthogonal persistence and compile to WebAssembly. The compiler and tooling were open-sourced in 2021.
Motoko.releasedEvent: Motoko introduced with the first public DFINITY Canister SDK (Copper release, late 2019)

NetRexx.creator: Mike Cowlishaw (IBM)
NetRexx.history: Mike Cowlishaw, who designed Rexx, began NetRexx in 1995 after porting Java to OS/2 and experimenting with running Rexx on the JVM. It brings Rexx's readable syntax to the Java platform with full access to Java classes, and was one of the first alternative JVM languages. IBM gave the source to RexxLA in 2011.
NetRexx.releasedEvent: NetRexx 0.50 released by IBM (1.00 followed in January 1997)

PARI/GP.creator: Henri Cohen et al. (Université de Bordeaux)
PARI/GP.history: PARI/GP was started around 1985 by Henri Cohen's team at Bordeaux, following the earlier Isabelle interpreter. PARI began as a library for Pascal ARIthmetic, a pun on Pascal's Wager, before moving to C, and GP was first called GPC, the Great Programmable Calculator. It is widely used in algebraic number theory and elliptic curve computations.
PARI/GP.releasedEvent: Development begun by Henri Cohen's team at Laboratoire A2X, Bordeaux

Pyret.creator: Brown PLT (Joe Gibbs Politz, Ben Lerner, Daniel Patterson, Shriram Krishnamurthi et al.)
Pyret.history: Pyret was developed by the PLT group at Brown University as a language for teaching programming, and was tested early on by students in Brown and Swarthmore courses. It mixes Python-like syntax with ideas from Racket and ML, puts test blocks and optional annotations directly into the language, and is used by the Bootstrap curricula and the DCIC textbook.
Pyret.releasedEvent: First commit of the brownplt/pyret-lang repository (no announcement found)

Q.creator: Arthur Whitney (Kx Systems)
Q.history: Q was written by Arthur Whitney at Kx Systems as a more readable, word-based layer over the K language, to query the kdb+ column-store database. Its lineage runs from APL through A+ and K. It is a staple for storing and analysing tick data in investment banks and trading firms.
Q.releasedEvent: q released by Kx Systems together with kdb+

Reason.creator: Jordan Walke (Facebook)
Reason.history: Reason was created at Facebook by Jordan Walke, who also created React. It gives OCaml a syntax familiar to JavaScript developers, and by September 2017 half of the Messenger web client's code had been converted to it. Its BuckleScript JavaScript toolchain later split off as ReScript.

Ring.creator: Mahmoud Samir Fayed
Ring.history: Ring was designed by Mahmoud Fayed, starting in September 2013, as the base for a rewrite of his visual programming tool PWCT (Programming Without Coding Technology). It is a small dynamic language with natural-language and declarative programming features, and ships with Qt and game library bindings.

Seed7.creator: Thomas Mertes
Seed7.history: Seed7 grew out of MASTER, an extensible language Thomas Mertes described in his 1984 diploma thesis and 1986 doctoral thesis at the Vienna University of Technology; work on its interpreter HAL began in 1989. Released as open source in 2005, Seed7 defines its statements and operators in libraries, so programmers can add new ones.
Seed7.releasedEvent: seed7_05_20051024.tgz, the earliest archive in the SourceForge file listing (project registered 2005-10-20)

Teal.creator: Hisham Muhammad
Teal.history: Hisham Muhammad, author of LuaRocks and htop, started the tl compiler in January 2019 after a FOSDEM talk on adding types to Lua, and presented it as working at FOSDEM 2020; the language was later named Teal. It adds static types to Lua and compiles to plain Lua, so it runs anywhere Lua does.
Teal.releasedEvent: tl v0.1.0 tagged on GitHub, the day of Hisham Muhammad's FOSDEM 2020 talk "Minimalistic typed Lua is here"

Underload.creator: Alex Smith (ais523)
Underload.history: Underload was created by Alex Smith (ais523) as a minimal stack-based language whose only data type is a string of commands. With a handful of single-character commands, including concatenation, quoting and eval, it is Turing complete and a classic example of a concatenative esolang.
Underload.releasedEvent: Underload page published on esolangs.org by its author ais523

Unison.creator: Paul Chiusano, Rúnar Bjarnason & Arya Irani (Unison Computing)
Unison.history: Unison began in 2013 as a research project by Paul Chiusano and is developed by Unison Computing, a public benefit corp he cofounded with Rúnar Bjarnason and Arya Irani. Definitions are identified by a hash of their syntax tree rather than stored as text files, which removes builds and dependency conflicts and makes distributed computing easier. Unison 1.0 was released in November 2025.
Unison.releasedEvent: First public alpha release (Milestone M1) of the Unison Codebase Manager published on GitHub

Unlambda.creator: David Madore
Unlambda.history: Unlambda was created by David Madore as an obfuscated functional language built on the S and K combinators of combinatory logic, with no variables or lambda operator. Every program is a chain of applications written with backquotes, and the original interpreter was written in Scheme.
Unlambda.releasedEvent: Announced by David Madore on the comp.lang.functional Usenet group; version 2.0.0 followed on 1999-12-20

Vim script.creator: Bram Moolenaar
Vim script.history: Vim script grew out of Vim's Ex command language and became a full scripting language with Vim 5.0 in 1998. Thousands of editor plugins are written in it, and Vim 9.0 in 2022 introduced the faster, typed Vim9 script.
Vim script.releasedEvent: Vim 5.0 released, adding user-defined functions and scripting

XSLT.creator: W3C (James Clark, editor)
XSLT.history: XSLT 1.0 was published by the W3C in November 1999 with James Clark as editor. It is a declarative, functional language written in XML for transforming XML documents, and it drives publishing toolchains such as DocBook and DITA.
XSLT.releasedEvent: XSLT 1.0 published as a W3C Recommendation

YueScript.creator: Li Jin
YueScript.history: YueScript was created by Li Jin, first as MoonPlus, a C++ reimplementation of the MoonScript compiler that was renamed YueScript in 2021. It adds pipes, destructuring and macros while still compiling to Lua, and it is developed alongside the Dora SSR game engine, where it is a main scripting language.
YueScript.releasedEvent: MoonPlus (the C++ MoonScript compiler later renamed YueScript) released as a library; renamed YueScript on 2021-02-17

Berry.creator: Guan Wenliang
Berry.history: Guan Wenliang wrote Berry as an ultra-lightweight scripting language for microcontrollers, borrowing parts of its design from Lua. Its one-pass compiler and register-based VM run in under 40 KiB of code and a few KiB of heap. It became the scripting language of the Tasmota firmware for ESP32 smart-home devices.
Berry.releasedEvent: First commit of the Berry repository (2018-11-11); version 0.0.1 builds dated December 2018

Umka.creator: Vasiliy Tereshkov
Umka.history: Vasiliy Tereshkov created Umka as an embeddable scripting language with Go-like syntax and static typing, so type errors are caught at compile time before the bytecode runs. Its motto, borrowed from the Zen of Python, is "explicit is better than implicit". Umka 1.0 came out in 2023, and it is the scripting language of the Tophat 2D game framework.
Umka.releasedEvent: v0.1-alpha release published on GitHub (announced on Habr 2020-05-09)

Scilab.creator: Scilab Group (INRIA and ENPC)
Scilab.history: Scilab grew out of Blaise, a control-systems design tool written at IRIA by François Delebecque and Serge Steer and renamed Basile in 1984. The six-researcher Scilab Group at INRIA and ENPC put Scilab 1.1 on an FTP site in January 1994. It is a MATLAB-like environment for numerical computing, with the Xcos block-diagram simulator.
Scilab.releasedEvent: Scilab 1.1, the first released version, put on an anonymous FTP site

KornShell.creator: David Korn (Bell Labs)
KornShell.history: The KornShell was written by David Korn at Bell Labs in the early 1980s. It combined Bourne shell compatibility with C shell interactive features, and ksh88 served as a basis for the POSIX shell standard. It is the default shell on AIX, and AT&T released ksh93 as open source in 2005.
KornShell.releasedEvent: Announced at the USENIX conference in Toronto

rc.creator: Tom Duff (Bell Labs)
rc.history: rc was written by Tom Duff, of Duff's device fame, at Bell Labs as the shell for Tenth Edition Unix and Plan 9. It draws heavily on the Bourne shell but replaces its quoting with a single-quote scheme, where a quote inside a string is written twice, and uses C-like control structures. Byron Rakitzis later reimplemented it for Unix.
rc.releasedEvent: Shell of Tenth Edition Unix and Plan 9

Gravity.creator: Marco Bambini (Creo)
Gravity.history: Marco Bambini wrote Gravity from scratch as the scripting engine of Creo, a Mac tool for building iOS and Android apps. It is a small class-based language with Swift-like syntax, written in C99 with no dependencies. Its closures follow Lua and its fibers and garbage collector draw on Bob Nystrom's Wren.
Gravity.releasedEvent: Open-source beta published on GitHub (repository created 2017-02-24; reported by Le Monde Informatique on 2017-03-13)

Harbour.creator: Antonio Linares et al.
Harbour.history: Antonio Linares founded Harbour in 1999 as a free, cross-platform compiler for the Clipper/xBase language used in many DOS business applications; the name plays on Clipper ships and ports. Viktor Szakáts and Przemysław Czerpak later redesigned it. It keeps old Clipper code running on modern systems and adds objects and multithreading.
Harbour.releasedEvent: Implementation started as an open project

PureBasic.creator: Frédéric Laboureur (Fantaisie Software)
PureBasic.history: PureBasic was created by Frédéric Laboureur, first for the Amiga in 1998 and then for Windows, whose first public release followed on 17 December 2000; Linux and macOS versions came later. It compiles a BASIC dialect to small native executables without runtime dependencies, and early licences still entitle owners to free upgrades.
PureBasic.releasedEvent: First commercial version released for the Amiga

Modula-2.creator: Niklaus Wirth (ETH Zurich)
Modula-2.history: Niklaus Wirth designed Modula-2 at ETH Zurich in 1977 to 1979 as Pascal's successor, adding modules with separate interfaces and low-level facilities. It was the language of the Lilith workstation's operating system and software, in daily use by 1980. GNU Modula-2 became part of GCC with version 13 in 2023.
Modula-2.releasedEvent: Modula-2 report published at ETH Zurich

Pyth.creator: Isaac Grosof (isaacg)
Pyth.history: Pyth was created by Isaac Grosof, known as isaacg on the Code Golf Stack Exchange, for code golf. Unlike stack-based golfing languages it is procedural and compiles to Python, with single-character commands that map onto Python features; an unterminated string at the end of a program is printed automatically.
Pyth.releasedEvent: Initial commit of the isaacg1/pyth repository on GitHub

Jelly.creator: Dennis Mitchell
Jelly.history: Jelly is a code golf language by Dennis Mitchell, inspired by J and built around tacit chains of links. It uses its own 256-character code page so that each symbol counts as a single byte. It is a regular in code golf answers and can be run on Try It Online.
Jelly.releasedEvent: Official repository DennisMitchell/jellylanguage created with first commit (no announcement found)

05AB1E.creator: Adnan (Adriandmen)
05AB1E.history: 05AB1E is a stack-based code golf language by PPCG user Adnan. Read as a hexadecimal number and converted to base64, the name gives "Base", because it was first meant to excel at base conversion before growing into a general golfing language. The current interpreter is written in Elixir.
05AB1E.releasedEvent: Initial commit of the 05AB1E repository on GitHub

Pkl.creator: Apple
Pkl.history: Apple open-sourced Pkl in February 2024 as a configuration language that sits between static formats like JSON and YAML and general-purpose languages. It adds classes, functions, type annotations with constraints and templating by amending, and validates values before deployment. It renders to JSON, YAML, XML and property lists and generates Swift, Go, Java and Kotlin code.

Vale.creator: Evan Ovadia
Vale.history: Vale is an experimental systems language by Evan Ovadia (Verdagon). Instead of a garbage collector or a borrow checker it uses generational references and region borrow checking to stay memory safe while staying fast and simple. Version 0.2 came out in May 2022, and the project was later archived in favour of its successor, Valen.
Vale.releasedEvent: Public GitHub repository (created 2020-06-28) and vale.dev site (archived from 2020-09) appear; version 0.1 completed in 2021

Self.creator: David Ungar and Randall B. Smith (Xerox PARC)
famousProjects: Self VM (JIT techniques reused in Java HotSpot)
Self.history: David Ungar and Randall B. Smith designed Self at Xerox PARC in 1986 as a simpler Smalltalk without classes: objects inherit directly from other objects. Work continued at Stanford and Sun until 1995. Its prototype model shaped JavaScript, and its adaptive compiler research led to the Java HotSpot VM.
Self.releasedEvent: First public release of the Self system (Stanford); language first published in the OOPSLA '87 paper "Self: The Power of Simplicity" (October 1987)

Retro.creator: Charles Childers (after Tom Novelli's original Retro)
Retro.history: Retro grew out of a Forth by Tom Novelli, who wrote Retro 1 to 4; Charles Childers took it over in 2001 and has developed it since. Retro 10 moved it from x86 assembly to the portable Ngaro virtual machine, and Retro 12 runs on the simpler Nga VM. Underscores in string literals stand for spaces.
Retro.releasedEvent: Charles Childers took over development of Retro from Tom Novelli

jq.creator: Stephen Dolan
famousProjects: Shell scripts and CI pipelines everywhere
jq.history: jq was written by Stephen Dolan as a sed-like tool for JSON. It is a small functional language of filters and pipes; run with -n and -r, a program that is just a string prints that string. The project is now maintained by the jqlang organization.
jq.releasedEvent: jq 1.0 tagged in the official repository (development began 2012-07-18)

Hylo.creator: Dimitri Racordon & Dave Abrahams
Hylo.history: Hylo, first named Val, grew out of Dimitri Racordon's research on mutable value semantics with Dave Abrahams, known for C++ and Swift standard library work. Memory safety comes from value semantics, without a garbage collector or pervasive references. It was presented publicly in 2022 and later renamed Hylo.
Hylo.releasedEvent: Val language presented publicly (C++Now 2022 keynote and CppCon 2022 talk); later renamed Hylo

Xtend.creator: Sven Efftinge and Sebastian Zarnekow (itemis, Eclipse)
Xtend.history: Xtend was created at itemis for the Eclipse Xtext project, first as Xtend2 to distinguish it from an older Xpand language of the same name. It compiles to readable Java source and adds lambdas, extension methods, type inference and template expressions on top of the Java type system. It became a standalone Eclipse project in 2012.
Xtend.releasedEvent: First released (as Xtend2) with Xtext 2.0 in the Eclipse Indigo release train

Frege.creator: Ingo Wechsung
Frege.history: Frege, named after the logician Gottlob Frege, is a pure lazy functional language in the Haskell tradition created by Ingo Wechsung. After a Perl prototype and a Java rewrite, he redesigned it as a Haskell subset and published it in 2011. It compiles to Java and calls Java libraries with types that track side effects.
Frege.releasedEvent: Frege (third redesign, a Haskell subset) published on Google Code

Miranda.creator: David Turner (Research Software Ltd.)
Miranda.history: David Turner designed Miranda in 1983 to 1986, and Research Software Ltd. sold it from 1985. Its lazy evaluation, pattern matching and polymorphic type inference made it the most widely used lazy functional language until the Haskell committee set out to create an open alternative. A BSD-licensed open-source release followed in 2020.
Miranda.releasedEvent: First release by Research Software Ltd. (interpreter in C for Unix)

Shen.creator: Mark Tarver
famousProjects: Shen ports to many host languages
Shen.history: Mark Tarver created Shen as the successor to his language Qi, with portability as the main goal: it is defined on a small kernel Lisp called KLambda, so it can be ported to many host languages. It offers pattern matching, an optional sequent-calculus type system and an embedded Prolog.
Shen.releasedEvent: Shen released as the successor to Qi

Assembly (RISC-V).creator: UC Berkeley (Krste Asanović, Yunsup Lee, Andrew Waterman, David Patterson)
Assembly (RISC-V).history: RISC-V started at UC Berkeley in 2010 as a clean, free instruction set architecture. Anyone can build RISC-V chips without licence fees, and it is now used from tiny microcontrollers to Linux-capable application processors.

Assembly (MIPS).creator: John L. Hennessy (Stanford, MIPS Computer Systems)
Assembly (MIPS).history: MIPS came out of John Hennessy's Stanford research into simple, pipelined RISC processors, and the R2000 shipped in 1985. MIPS CPUs powered SGI workstations, the Nintendo 64 and the first two PlayStations, and MIPS assembly is still a standard teaching language with the SPIM and MARS simulators.

FreeBASIC.creator: Andre Victor T. Vicentini
FreeBASIC.history: Andre Victor began FreeBASIC in late summer 2004 as a free 32-bit compiler, first written in Visual Basic for DOS until it could compile itself. It keeps QuickBASIC syntax working through a 'qb' dialect while adding pointers, objects, operator overloading and direct access to C libraries.
FreeBASIC.releasedEvent: First compiler versions (work began late summer 2004)

Small Basic.creator: Vijaye Raji (Microsoft)
Small Basic.history: Vijaye Raji developed Small Basic part-time at Microsoft for nearly a year before its release in October 2008, to make text programming approachable for beginners coming from tools like Scratch. It has only 14 keywords, an editor with IntelliSense and a turtle-graphics library, and is used in many school courses.
Small Basic.releasedEvent: Vijaye Raji's "Hello World" post announcing the first Small Basic release (v0.1) on the Small Basic blog

GameMaker Language.creator: Mark Overmars
GameMaker Language.history: GML is the scripting language of GameMaker, which Mark Overmars first released in 1999 as Animo, a graphics tool with limited visual scripting. The language grew over the following versions alongside the drag-and-drop actions. Indie hits such as Undertale, Hotline Miami and the original Spelunky were written in it.
GameMaker Language.releasedEvent: First release of GameMaker, under the name Animo

AngelScript.creator: Andreas Jönsson (AngelCode)
AngelScript.history: AngelScript was created by Andreas Jönsson as a scripting language that C++ programs can embed with little binding glue: its syntax and types are close to C++. Games such as Amnesia: The Dark Descent, Overgrowth and SuperTuxKart use it for gameplay logic.
AngelScript.releasedEvent: Version 0.1, the first entry in the official AngelScript changelog

Maxima.creator: William Schelter (based on MIT Macsyma)
Maxima.history: Maxima descends from Macsyma, developed at MIT from the late 1960s. William Schelter maintained a 1982 version of DOE Macsyma until his death in 2001, and in 1998 got permission to release it under the GPL. An independent group of users and developers has maintained it since.
Maxima.releasedEvent: William Schelter began maintaining the 1982 DOE version of Macsyma that became Maxima (GPL release permitted in 1998)

GAP.creator: Joachim Neubüser et al. (RWTH Aachen)
GAP.history: GAP (Groups, Algorithms, Programming) was started in 1986 at Lehrstuhl D für Mathematik, RWTH Aachen, under Joachim Neubüser, with the first public release in 1988. Coordination moved to St Andrews in 1997 and later to several GAP Centres. It is the standard open-source system for computational group theory and discrete algebra.
GAP.releasedEvent: GAP 2.4, the first publicly released version

Magma.creator: John Cannon (Computational Algebra Group, University of Sydney)
Magma.history: Magma was developed by John Cannon's Computational Algebra Group at the University of Sydney as the successor to Cayley, which was used from 1982 to 1993. It is named after the algebraic structure. Magma is a commercial system known for fast algorithms in group theory, number theory, algebraic geometry and coding theory.

SageMath.creator: William Stein (University of Washington)
SageMath.history: SageMath was started by William Stein, then at the University of Washington, as an open-source alternative to Magma, Maple, Mathematica and MATLAB. Rather than rewrite existing tools, it combines GAP, PARI, Maxima, NumPy and many other packages behind a Python-based language. It received the ACM SIGSAM Jenks Prize in 2013.
SageMath.releasedEvent: First version of Sage released under the GPL

Arturo.creator: Yanis Zafirópulos
Arturo.history: Arturo was created by Yanis Zafirópulos (Dr.Kameleon) as a batteries-included scripting language with very little syntax, related to Rebol, Forth, Logo and Ruby. It started as an experiment and its interpreter is written in Nim.
Arturo.releasedEvent: v0.3.1, the first GitHub release of the Nim implementation

Ink.creator: inkle (Joseph Humfrey, Jon Ingold)
Ink.history: Ink is the scripting language inkle built for its narrative games such as 80 Days and Sorcery!, and open-sourced under the MIT license in 2016. Plain text is printed as story text, so a line on its own is a complete program; choices, knots and variables add branching. Version 1.0 arrived in 2021.

Inform 6.creator: Graham Nelson
Inform 6.history: Inform 6 is the 1996 rewrite of Graham Nelson's language for interactive fiction, which he first released in 1993. It compiles to the Z-machine format of Infocom's classic games (and to Glulx), and ^ in strings means a newline. It is still maintained, and Inform 7 compiles through it.

Jule.creator: Mertcan Davulcu
Jule.history: Jule is a statically typed, compiled language started by Mertcan Davulcu. It aims for simplicity and safety by default, with bounds checking, reference counting, built-in concurrency and first-class C and C++ interoperability. Its compiler is bootstrapped, written in Jule itself.
Jule.releasedEvent: First commit in the official julelang/jule repository; first beta release jule-beta-0.0.1 on 2023-07-17

MoonBit.creator: Hongbo Zhang (International Digital Economy Academy)
MoonBit.history: MoonBit was announced in August 2023 by a team at the International Digital Economy Academy led by Hongbo Zhang, who previously worked on OCaml, Flow and the ReScript toolchain. Designed as a Wasm-first language, it compiles to compact WebAssembly as well as JavaScript and native code, and ships with its own build tool and IDE.
MoonBit.releasedEvent: Public announcement of MoonBit with an online web IDE (alpha)

Rebol.creator: Carl Sassenrath
Rebol.history: Rebol was designed by Carl Sassenrath, architect of the Amiga's operating system, as a messaging language for exchanging data and running small tasks across the network. Programs are blocks of words that small domain-specific dialects interpret, an idea that the Red language continues. Rebol 3 was open-sourced under the Apache licence in December 2012.
Rebol.releasedEvent: REBOL/Core alpha distributed to testers on the email announcement list (late 1997)

tcsh.creator: Ken Greer (Carnegie Mellon University)
tcsh.history: Ken Greer started adding TENEX-style file name completion to the C shell at Carnegie Mellon, merged it in 1981, and posted it to Usenet in October 1983; the t comes from TENEX. Paul Placeway and others later added line editing. It was the default shell on early Mac OS X and for root on FreeBSD.
tcsh.releasedEvent: Ken Greer posted the C shell with command and file name completion to net.sources

Xonsh.creator: Anthony Scopatz
Xonsh.history: Xonsh was created by Anthony Scopatz as a shell whose language is a superset of Python. Shell commands and Python expressions mix freely and compile to Python, so scripts get Python data structures and libraries. Scopatz presented it to a wide audience at PyCon 2016.

YSH.creator: Andy Chu (Oils project)
YSH.history: YSH is the new shell language of the Oils project started by Andy Chu, which also provides OSH, a bash-compatible shell. It first shipped in 2019 as the Oil language and was renamed YSH in 2023. YSH keeps shell commands but adds real data structures, JSON and Python-like expressions without bash's quoting traps.
YSH.releasedEvent: Oil 0.7.pre5 released and announced as 'You Can Now Try the Oil Language'; renamed YSH in 2023

Picat.creator: Neng-Fa Zhou and Jonathan Fruhman
famousProjects: Winning entries in LP/CP programming contests
Picat.history: Picat was designed by Neng-Fa Zhou, with Jonathan Fruhman, and implemented on the B-Prolog engine; the name stands for Pattern-matching, Intuitive, Constraints, Actors and Tabling. It mixes logic programming, functions, pattern-matching rules and imperative loops, and ships with constraint, SAT and MIP solver modules. Picat entries place well in XCSP and MiniZinc solver competitions.
Picat.releasedEvent: First alpha version released (design published December 2012)

Neko.creator: Nicolas Cannasse (Motion Twin)
Neko.history: Nicolas Cannasse created Neko as part of research work at the Bordeaux game studio Motion Twin. It is a small dynamically typed language compiled to bytecode for the NekoVM, and it was one of the first targets of Haxe when Haxe's beta appeared in 2006. Built-in functions are prefixed with a dollar sign, as in $print.
Neko.releasedEvent: Neko 1.0 (tag v1-0 in the official repository; first commit 7 Jan 2005)

Golo.creator: Julien Ponge, Frédéric Le Mouël, Nicolas Stouls (DynaMid group, CITI Laboratory, INSA Lyon)
Golo.history: Golo was built by the DynaMid research group at INSA Lyon as a small dynamic language showing how to build a runtime on the JVM's invokedynamic instruction, and was open-sourced at Devoxx France in March 2013. It became an Eclipse Foundation project in 2015 and was terminated in 2022. Closures are written with a |args| parameter syntax.

Beef.creator: Brian Fiete (BeefyTech)
Beef.history: Beef was created by Brian Fiete, a co-founder of PopCap Games, who wanted C#'s developer experience with C++ performance for game code. It compiles to native code through an LLVM backend, detects memory leaks in real time, and ships with its own IDE, debugger and profiler.
Beef.releasedEvent: Version 0.42.1, the first tagged release on GitHub

Objeck.creator: Randy Hollines
Objeck.history: Objeck grew out of a 2008 prototype by Randy Hollines for translating stack VM instructions into register code and then machine code. The prototype became a small VM called StackVM with an assembler, and the project took the name Objeck when a full language frontend replaced the assembler. Programs compile to bytecode run by a VM with a garbage collector and JIT compiler.
Objeck.releasedEvent: Prototype begun (per project history); earliest public commit is 2010-02-27

Nit.creator: Jean Privat
Nit.history: Nit followed PRM (Programming with Refinement and Modules), the language of Jean Privat's 2006 doctoral thesis at LIRMM in Montpellier, and has been developed by Privat at the Université du Québec à Montréal. It is statically typed but keeps a light, script-like syntax, and it lets modules refine existing classes.
Nit.releasedEvent: 'First NIT release' commit by Jean Privat in the official repository

Zeek.creator: Vern Paxson (Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory)
Zeek.history: Zeek, known as Bro until 2018, was designed by Vern Paxson at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in 1995 and deployed there in 1996. His 1998 paper describing it won Best Paper at USENIX Security. Its domain-specific scripting language reacts to network events; zeek_init is the event raised once when Zeek starts.
Zeek.releasedEvent: Vern Paxson's paper 'Bro: A System for Detecting Network Intruders in Real-Time' presented at the 7th USENIX Security Symposium

Rhai.creator: Sophia Turner
famousProjects: Scripting in Rust applications and game engines
Rhai.history: Rhai was started in 2016 as a small scripting language that Rust programs can embed without extra dependencies. It began as a Rust port of the ideas behind ChaiScript, with the C swapped for an R. It has a JavaScript- and Rust-like syntax, is sandboxed by default, and is now maintained by a community team.
Rhai.releasedEvent: Initial commit of the Rhai repository (no announcement found)

Rune.creator: John-John Tedro
Rune.history: Rune was started by John-John Tedro in 2020 as a dynamic language that feels like Rust without types and embeds cleanly into Rust programs, aiming to be about as fast and convenient as Lua. It runs on a stack-based virtual machine and supports async functions, generators and hot reloading.
Rune.releasedEvent: Initial commit of the rune-rs/rune repository by John-John Tedro (first GitHub release 0.7.0 on 2020-10-19)

Koto.creator: Ian Hobson
famousProjects: Scripting in Rust audio and creative tools
Koto.history: Koto was started by Ian Hobson in 2020 to be a scripting language for applications written in Rust, such as animation and game tools. It is indentation-based and expression-oriented, with Lua as a strong influence and a focus on iterators, and parentheses around function arguments are optional in simple calls.
Koto.releasedEvent: v0.1.0 tagged when the repository went public (first commit 2020-02-17)

ChaiScript.creator: Jason Turner & Jonathan Turner
ChaiScript.history: Jason Turner and Jonathan Turner released ChaiScript to make it trivially easy to add scripting to a C++ application. It is a header-only library, so C++ functions and types can be exposed to scripts without a bindings generator. Its syntax resembles JavaScript.
ChaiScript.releasedEvent: First ChaiScript release announced by Jason Turner on emptycrate.com

MiniScript.creator: Joe Strout
MiniScript.history: Joe Strout began MiniScript in late 2015 as a lightweight scripting language for Unity games, announcing it on the Unity forums in December 2015, and released it in 2017. It later gained a C++ version and powers the Mini Micro retro computer environment. Its syntax was designed to be learnable in minutes.

Terra.creator: Zachary DeVito, James Hegarty, Alex Aiken, Pat Hanrahan and Jan Vitek (Stanford University)
Terra.history: Terra came out of Zachary DeVito's research with Pat Hanrahan at Stanford and was presented at PLDI 2013. Terra functions are statically typed, compiled through LLVM and can call C directly, while the surrounding Lua code generates and stages them at runtime. The paper's BLAS auto-tuner ran within 20% of ATLAS.
Terra.releasedEvent: PLDI 2013 paper "Terra: A Multi-Stage Language for High-Performance Computing"

QBE.creator: Quentin Carbonneaux
QBE.history: QBE (Quick Backend) is a small compiler backend by Quentin Carbonneaux that aims for 70% of the performance of industrial optimizing compilers in 10% of the code. Its SSA-based intermediate language is compiled to assembly, which is then linked against the C library; this sample calls puts. It is the backend of the cproc C compiler and the Hare language.
QBE.releasedEvent: QBE announced by Quentin Carbonneaux on the suckless dev mailing list

CJam.creator: aditsu
CJam.history: aditsu created CJam in 2014 as a stack-based code-golf language inspired by GolfScript, with an interpreter written in Java. Whatever is left on the stack is printed when the program ends, so a lone string literal is a complete Hello World.
CJam.releasedEvent: CJam project registered on SourceForge (2014-04-08); first listed release 0.5 on 2014-04-11

FALSE.creator: Wouter van Oortmerssen
FALSE.history: FALSE was designed in 1993 by Wouter van Oortmerssen with the goal of writing a working compiler of just 1024 bytes, in 68000 assembler for the Amiga. It is a Forth-like stack language of single-character commands, and a string in double quotes is printed when it is reached. It inspired Brainfuck and Befunge.

BlitzMax.creator: Mark Sibly (Blitz Research)
BlitzMax.history: Mark Sibly's Blitz Research released BlitzMax as the object-oriented, cross-platform successor to Blitz Basic and Blitz3D, after a wait long enough that some suspected it was vaporware. It shipped first for Mac OS X with an OpenGL 2D engine. Open-sourced in 2015, it lives on as BlitzMax NG.
BlitzMax.releasedEvent: BlitzMax released for Mac OS X (reported by Slashdot on 2004-12-16); Windows and Linux followed in 2005

S-Lang.creator: John E. Davis
S-Lang.history: S-Lang was started in 1992 by John E. Davis, who turned functions from his JED text editor into a reusable library; its interpreter first had a PostScript-like syntax and later became C-like. Besides terminal and screen handling, used by slrn and Mutt, it provides an interpreted language with array operations, runnable on its own with the slsh shell since version 2.0.
S-Lang.releasedEvent: Library started by John E. Davis for the JED editor (no first release date found)

Daslang.creator: Boris Batkin (Gaijin Entertainment)
Daslang.history: Daslang, formerly daScript, was written by Boris Batkin at Gaijin Entertainment, where Lua and Squirrel interop costs were eating the frame budget. A prototype that avoided marshalling data beat LuaJIT's interpreter. It is statically typed, embeds in C++ game engines with near-native speed, and the [export] annotation makes main callable from the host.
Daslang.releasedEvent: Initial lexer committed to the daScript repository

Cpp2.creator: Herb Sutter
Cpp2.history: Cpp2 is an experimental alternative syntax for C++ that Herb Sutter presented at CppCon 2022, building on proposals he had made since 2015. His cppfront compiler translates it into ordinary C++, so Cpp2 code mixes freely with existing C++ libraries while defaulting to safer rules.
Cpp2.releasedEvent: Herb Sutter's CppCon 2022 talk 'Can C++ be 10x simpler and safer?' introduced Cpp2 and the cppfront compiler

Turing.creator: Ric Holt and James Cordy (University of Toronto)
Turing.history: Turing was designed in 1982 by Ric Holt and James Cordy at the University of Toronto as a language for students in their first programming course, and it was used widely in Ontario high schools. It descends from Pascal, Euclid and SP/k, and the put statement writes a line of output. Holt Software Associates stopped developing it in 2007.
Turing.releasedEvent: Turing developed and introduced at the University of Toronto

Tengo.creator: Daniel Kang
Tengo.history: Daniel Kang published Tengo in January 2019 as a fast script language for Go applications, naming it after Haruki Murakami's novel 1Q84. Scripts compile to bytecode that runs on a stack-based virtual machine written in pure Go. Standard library modules such as fmt are loaded with import.
Tengo.releasedEvent: First GitHub releases (v0.9.x, then v1.0.0 the same day) of d5/tengo

Thue.creator: John Colagioia
Thue.history: Thue was created by John Colagioia in 2000 and is based on semi-Thue string rewriting systems. A program is a list of rules written lhs::=rhs, closed by an empty rule and followed by the initial string. A right-hand side that starts with ~ prints its text instead of rewriting, and rules are applied in no fixed order until none match.

Whenever.creator: David Morgan-Mar
Whenever.history: Whenever is an esoteric language by David Morgan-Mar, the author of Chef and Piet. Every line is numbered and goes on a to-do list that the interpreter works through in random order, and there are no variables or flow control. print() writes its string followed by a newline.
Whenever.releasedEvent: Specification online on David Morgan-Mar's site (earliest archived copy August 2002)

Glass.creator: Gregor Richards
Glass.history: Glass was created by Gregor Richards in 2005. It mixes postfix notation with heavy object orientation: a program defines a main class M with a method m. Here an instance of the built-in output class O is stored in _o, the string is pushed onto the stack and _o.o prints it.

Felix.creator: John Skaller
Felix.history: Felix was created by John Skaller, and its SourceForge project dates from 2001. It is a statically typed language that is translated to C++ and compiled to native code, with direct embedding of C++ types and functions. The flx tool builds and runs a .flx file in one step, with no makefiles.

Dyon.creator: Sven Nilsen
Dyon.history: Dyon was started by Sven Nilsen in January 2016 as a scripting language for the Piston game engine community. It is dynamically typed but borrows much of its syntax from Rust, uses a lifetime checker instead of a garbage collector, and is built for embedding in Rust programs. Programs start at fn main().
Dyon.releasedEvent: Dyon repository created under PistonDevelopers on GitHub

Gluon.creator: Markus Westerlind
Gluon.history: Markus Westerlind began Gluon in August 2014 as a small, statically typed functional language for embedding in Rust applications, drawing on Lua, Haskell and OCaml. It has Hindley-Milner type inference, so types rarely need to be written, and each Gluon thread gets its own garbage-collected heap. Modules are loaded with the import! macro.

Lily.creator: FascinatedBox
Lily.history: Lily has been developed by FascinatedBox since 2011. It is statically typed, but its reference implementation is an interpreter designed for embedding and sandboxing, so several interpreters can run side by side. It has classes, enums and a |> pipe operator.
Lily.releasedEvent: First commit in the official repository history (no announcement found)

ELENA.creator: Alex (Aleksey) Rakov
ELENA.history: ELENA is a general-purpose language with late binding, developed by Alex (Aleksey) Rakov and first hosted on SourceForge. It combines object-oriented and functional features, with multi-methods, mixins and optional types. Programs start from a public Program function and compile for Windows, Linux, FreeBSD and macOS.

SETL.creator: Jacob T. Schwartz (Courant Institute, New York University)
famousProjects: Ada/Ed, the first validated Ada compiler
SETL.history: Jacob T. Schwartz designed SETL at New York University's Courant Institute around 1969 to 1970, with finite sets and tuples as its basic data structures. NYU's Ada/Ed, the first validated Ada translator, was written in SETL, and the language influenced ABC and through it Python. GNU SETL, hosted at setl.org, is a current implementation.
SETL.releasedEvent: Jacob T. Schwartz's Courant Institute report "Set theory as a language for program specification and programming" outlining SETL

BBC BASIC.creator: Sophie Wilson (Acorn Computers)
BBC BASIC.history: BBC BASIC was written by Sophie Wilson at Acorn Computers in 1981 for the BBC Micro. It added ALGOL-style named procedures and functions and an inline assembler to BASIC, and it later shipped with RISC OS. Richard Russell's BBC BASIC for Windows and BBC BASIC for SDL keep it in use today.
BBC BASIC.releasedEvent: Released with Acorn's BBC Micro for the BBC Computer Literacy Project

Oxygene.creator: marc hoffman and Carlo Kok (RemObjects Software)
Oxygene.history: In 2005 marc hoffman and Carlo Kok of RemObjects created Chrome, an Object Pascal for .NET, in response to the direction of Delphi for .NET; it was later renamed Oxygene. Embarcadero licensed it as Delphi Prism from 2008 to 2012. Part of the Elements compiler, it now targets .NET, Java, Android, Apple platforms, WebAssembly and native Windows and Linux.
Oxygene.releasedEvent: First released as Chrome by RemObjects Software

IDL.creator: David Stern (Research Systems Inc.)
IDL.history: David Stern wrote IDL (Interactive Data Language) for analysing space science data, after earlier tools at the University of Colorado's LASP, and founded Research Systems in 1977 to develop it; the first licenses were sold in 1979. It is an array-oriented language used in astronomy, remote sensing and medical imaging, now sold by NV5 Geospatial. GDL is a free implementation.
IDL.releasedEvent: Research Systems Inc. founded by David Stern, with IDL for the PDP-11 as its first product

Macaulay2.creator: Daniel Grayson and Michael Stillman
Macaulay2.history: Daniel Grayson and Michael Stillman created Macaulay2, with NSF funding from 1992 and first releases in 1993, as a successor to the Macaulay system. It is a computer algebra system and language for research in commutative algebra and algebraic geometry. A script runs with M2 --script, and print writes a value followed by a newline.

Sidef.creator: Daniel Șuteu
Sidef.history: Daniel Șuteu (trizen) started Sidef in 2013 and implemented it in Perl. It combines ideas from Ruby, Raku and Perl with exact rational arithmetic and a large set of built-in number-theory functions, and can use Perl modules. say prints its argument followed by a newline.
Sidef.releasedEvent: Initial commit of the public GitHub repository trizen/sidef (first tagged release 0.01 on 2014-05-25)

Frink.creator: Alan Eliasen
Frink.history: Frink was created by Alan Eliasen around 2001 and runs on the Java virtual machine; it is named after Professor Frink from The Simpsons. It tracks units of measure through every calculation, so quantities such as feet, meters and watts can be mixed and checked automatically. Function calls use square brackets, as in println[...].

LDPL.creator: Martín del Río (Lartu)
LDPL.history: LDPL was created by Lartu in 2019 as a readable, COBOL-inspired language whose compiler translates programs to C++. Programs are split into a data section and a procedure section, and every statement does exactly one thing. display writes its arguments, and crlf adds a line break. The sample uses the syntax of LDPL 5.1, the latest release; the 5.2 development version writes the section header as PROCEDURE without the colon.

HQ9+.creator: Cliff Biffle
HQ9+.history: HQ9+ is a joke language created by Cliff Biffle in 2001 with four commands: H prints a greeting, Q prints the program's source, 9 prints the lyrics of 99 Bottles of Beer and + increments an accumulator. The program H prints "Hello, world!", with a lowercase w, as the original specification says.
HQ9+.releasedEvent: Specification page published on Cliff Biffle's site

OpenSCAD.creator: Claire Wolf and Marius Kintel
OpenSCAD.history: OpenSCAD was started by Claire Wolf (then Clifford Wolf) and developed with Marius Kintel, who maintains it, with a first release in February 2010. Its language describes 3D solids through constructive solid geometry and extrusion, and it is widely used for parametric 3D-printing models. echo() writes to the console with a prefix, so this program prints ECHO: "Hello, World!".

MiniZinc.creator: Nicholas Nethercote, Peter J. Stuckey, Ralph Becket, Sebastian Brand, Gregory J. Duck & Guido Tack (NICTA G12 project)
MiniZinc.history: MiniZinc was introduced in 2007 by the G12 team at NICTA and the University of Melbourne, including Nicholas Nethercote and Peter J. Stuckey, as a standard modelling language for constraint programming. A model is compiled to FlatZinc and handed to any of many solvers; development continues at Monash University. A model may have no variables and no solve item, in which case it is a satisfaction problem; after printing the output item, MiniZinc adds a line of ten dashes (----------) to mark the solution.
MiniZinc.releasedEvent: MiniZinc 0.6 released with the G12 project and presented in the CP 2007 paper "MiniZinc: Towards a Standard CP Modelling Language"

Rocq.creator: Thierry Coquand & Gérard Huet (INRIA)
Rocq.history: Rocq began at INRIA as Coq, an implementation of Thierry Coquand's Calculus of Constructions started with Gérard Huet in 1984, with the first public release, version 4.10, in 1989; the rename to Rocq was completed with version 9.0 in March 2025. It is used to write machine-checked proofs, such as the CompCert verified C compiler and the four colour theorem. Compute evaluates the string and prints it with its type, as = "Hello, World!" : string.
Rocq.releasedEvent: Coq version 4.10, the first public release

Meson.creator: Jussi Pakkanen
Meson.history: Meson was created by Jussi Pakkanen and first released in March 2013 as a fast, user-friendly build system that generates Ninja files. Its build files, named meson.build, use a small Python-like language that is deliberately not Turing complete. Running meson setup on this file prints Message: Hello, World! while configuring the project.

Apex.creator: Salesforce
Apex.history: Apex was announced by Salesforce at its Dreamforce conference in October 2006 as a Java-like language that runs on Salesforce's multi-tenant servers; a developer preview followed and it became generally available in 2007. It is strongly typed and object-oriented, and it is used for triggers, controllers and other business logic on the platform. This line runs as anonymous Apex, and System.debug writes the text to the debug log as a USER_DEBUG entry.
Apex.releasedEvent: Apex announced and previewed at Dreamforce 2006; generally available with the Summer '07 release

PL/pgSQL.creator: Jan Wieck
PL/pgSQL.history: PL/pgSQL was written by Jan Wieck and shipped with PostgreSQL 6.4 in October 1998. It adds variables, loops, conditions and exception handling to SQL for writing functions, procedures and triggers inside the database, in a style close to Oracle's PL/SQL. The DO statement runs an anonymous code block, and RAISE NOTICE sends the message to the client, which psql shows as NOTICE:  Hello, World!

Promela.creator: Gerard J. Holzmann (Bell Labs)
Promela.history: Promela (Process Meta Language) is the input language of the SPIN model checker, which Gerard J. Holzmann developed in the Unix group at Bell Labs from 1980 and has made freely available since 1991. It describes concurrent processes that communicate through channels, so that SPIN can check the design for deadlocks and other errors. The init process plays the role of main in C; spin prints the text and then reports 1 process created.
Promela.releasedEvent: SPIN model checker, with Promela as its input language, made freely available

RPG.creator: IBM
RPG.history: RPG (Report Program Generator) was introduced by IBM with the IBM 1401 in 1959 to let former tabulating-machine programmers produce business reports from punched-card data. Its current form, ILE RPG (RPG IV), runs on IBM i and is still widely used for business systems; the **free line switches the source to fully free-form syntax. The DSPLY operation shows the message on the job's message line, as DSPLY  Hello, World!
RPG.releasedEvent: Report Program Generator described among the programming systems in IBM's 1959 IBM 1401 brochure

TADS 3.creator: Michael J. Roberts
TADS 3.history: TADS (Text Adventure Development System) was created by Michael J. Roberts and first released as shareware in 1988. TADS 3, a complete redesign with a new language and virtual machine, had its first beta in 2004 and its first general release in September 2006. It is used to write parser-based interactive fiction, usually with the adv3 library. A double-quoted string on its own is a statement that displays the text; t3make compiles the program and t3run runs it.

Ioke.creator: Ola Bini
Ioke.history: Ioke was created by Ola Bini, a JRuby developer, who described it on the jvm-languages list in April 2008 and released the first version, Ioke 0, that December. It is a dynamic, prototype-based and homoiconic language for the Java virtual machine, influenced by Io, Smalltalk, Lisp and Ruby. Messages are sent by juxtaposition, so println is sent to the string.
Ioke.releasedEvent: Ioke 0, the first release, announced by Ola Bini

Yabasic.creator: Marc-Oliver Ihm
Yabasic.history: Yabasic (Yet Another BASIC) was written by Marc-Oliver Ihm, who released version 1.0 around May 1995 after reading Niklaus Wirth's book on compiler construction. Version 2.0 added a Windows port in 1996 and version 2.57 added subroutines and libraries in 1999, and it has simple graphics commands. Sony shipped a version of it on the demo disc of PAL PlayStation 2 consoles.

Nickle.creator: Keith Packard & Bart Massey
Nickle.history: Nickle was developed by Keith Packard and Bart Massey from a calculator language they had worked on intermittently for about twenty years, and it was presented at the 2001 USENIX FREENIX conference. Its syntax resembles C, and it supports many data types, especially arbitrary-precision numbers. It is used as a desktop calculator and for prototyping numerical algorithms.
Nickle.releasedEvent: Presented in the paper "Nickle: Language Principles and Pragmatics" at the 2001 USENIX FREENIX track

Pure.creator: Albert Gräf (University of Mainz)
Pure.history: Pure was created by Albert Gräf at the University of Mainz and first released in April 2008 as the successor to his Q language. Programs are sets of equations that are evaluated by term rewriting, and the interpreter compiles them to native code through LLVM. The system module provides puts, which calls C's puts and writes the string with a newline.

Quackery.creator: Gordon Charlton
