Quackery.history: Quackery was published by Gordon Charlton in December 2020 as a lightweight language for recreational and educational programming, inspired by Forth and Lisp. Its processor and a basic compiler are written in Python 3, and it is meant as a gentle introduction to concatenative programming. say prints the string that follows it, and cr ends the line.
Quackery.releasedEvent: Quackery repository published on GitHub (initial commit 2020-12-01)

min.creator: Fabio Cevasco
min.history: min was created by Fabio Cevasco; its repository dates from 2014 and it was announced publicly at the end of July 2017. It is a functional, concatenative language with a minimal syntax, written in Nim and distributed as a single executable with an advanced REPL; its author also uses it to script his HastySite static site generator. puts prints the value on top of the stack followed by a newline.
min.releasedEvent: "Show HN: Min programming language" public announcement

Wenyan.creator: Lingdong Huang
Wenyan.history: Wenyan (文言) was created by Lingdong Huang, who finished its core during his last month as a student at Carnegie Mellon, and released it in December 2019. It follows the grammar and tone of Classical Chinese literature and compiles to JavaScript, Python or Ruby. Its own hello world, used here, prints 問天地好在。 (roughly "I ask heaven and earth whether they are well"): 書之 writes the string declared before it.
Wenyan.releasedEvent: Published on GitHub and announced on Hacker News (v0.0.1 tagged 2019-12-20)

ABC.creator: Leo Geurts, Lambert Meertens & Steven Pemberton (CWI)
ABC.history: ABC was developed at CWI in Amsterdam by Leo Geurts, Lambert Meertens and Steven Pemberton as a simple, interactive replacement for BASIC, growing out of Meertens and Pemberton's earlier language B, and it was introduced in 1987. Guido van Rossum worked on the ABC system in the mid-1980s, and it was a major influence on Python. In WRITE, a slash starts a new line.
ABC.releasedEvent: Introduced in Steven Pemberton's IEEE Software article "An Alternative Simple Language and Environment for PCs"

Bluespec.creator: Lennart Augustsson, from research by Arvind and James Hoe (MIT)
Bluespec.history: Bluespec grew out of 1990s research by James Hoe and Arvind at MIT on compiling hardware from rules; in 2000 Lennart Augustsson implemented it as BH (Bluespec Haskell, or Bluespec Classic), and Bluespec Inc. added the SystemVerilog-style syntax (BSV) used here in 2004-2005. Hardware is described as rules, guarded atomic actions that the compiler schedules. The compiler was open-sourced in January 2020, and $display prints when the rule fires in simulation.
Bluespec.releasedEvent: Lennart Augustsson implements the first Bluespec language (BH, Bluespec Haskell) at Sandburst

Brachylog.creator: Julien Cumin
Brachylog.history: Brachylog was created by Julien Cumin in 2015 as a declarative logic programming language that is much terser than Prolog, mainly for code golf; a rewritten version 2 followed in 2017. Its interpreter is written in Prolog and transpiles programs to Prolog for SWI-Prolog. w writes its argument; the sample is the one the project's README uses.
Brachylog.releasedEvent: Brachylog repository published on GitHub (initial commit 2015-08-26)

Japt.creator: ETHproductions
Japt.history: Japt was created by the code golfer ETHproductions in 2015 as a shortened form of JavaScript, into which it is transpiled; many methods are single letters and input and output are implicit. The value of the last expression is printed automatically, so a string literal is a complete hello world.
Japt.releasedEvent: Japt repository published on GitHub (2015-11-18); release v1.3 tagged 2015-11-23

B.creator: Ken Thompson & Dennis Ritchie (Bell Labs)
B.history: Ken Thompson created B at Bell Labs in 1969-70 as a stripped-down BCPL for the PDP-7, and Dennis Ritchie later grew it into C. It has a single data type, the machine word. This sample is adapted from Brian Kernighan's tutorial on B, whose original prints hello, world! in lower case: a word holds at most four characters, so the text is split across three external variables.
B.releasedEvent: Ken Thompson creates B at Bell Labs (1969-70)

Malbolge.creator: Ben Olmstead
Malbolge.history: Ben Olmstead invented Malbolge in 1998, naming it after the eighth circle of hell in Dante's Inferno, to be as difficult to program in as possible. It runs on a ternary virtual machine that encrypts each instruction after it executes, and the first hello world took two years to appear and was found by a search program. This shorter program prints Hello, world.
Malbolge.releasedEvent: Ben Olmstead publishes the language and its interpreter

SuperCollider.creator: James McCartney
SuperCollider.history: James McCartney released SuperCollider in 1996 for real-time audio synthesis and made it free software under the GPL in 2002. Its sclang language is object-oriented in the style of Smalltalk and sends commands to a separate synthesis server, scsynth. It is widely used for live coding and electronic music; postln prints the string in the post window.

TeX.creator: Donald Knuth
TeX.history: Donald Knuth began TeX in the late 1970s while revising the second volume of The Art of Computer Programming, because he was unhappy with the look of its new galleys. Its macro language is Turing complete, and its version number converges to pi, gaining one digit with each bug-fix release. This plain TeX file typesets one page with Hello, World! and the page number 1; \bye ends the job.

gnuplot.creator: Thomas Williams & Colin Kelley
gnuplot.history: Thomas Williams and Colin Kelley wrote gnuplot in 1986 to visualise the mathematics in their engineering courses. Despite its name it has no connection to the GNU Project; the name was a compromise between llamaplot and nplot. Its command language has variables, functions and loops, and print writes the text to the screen, on standard error by default.

Ren'Py.creator: Tom Rothamel
Ren'Py.history: Ren'Py was written by Tom "PyTom" Rothamel and first released in August 2004 as an engine for visual novels. Its scripts read like a screenplay and can drop into Python for anything more complex. A game starts at the start label, and a string on its own line is narration shown in the dialogue window.

Linden Scripting Language.creator: Linden Lab
Linden Scripting Language.history: LSL is the scripting language of Second Life, the virtual world that Linden Lab launched in 2003. Scripts are state machines with event handlers, and they run on the simulator servers, today compiled to the Mono runtime. When the object is created, the default state's state_entry event fires and llSay says the message on public chat channel 0 under the object's name.
Linden Scripting Language.releasedEvent: Second Life, which LSL scripts, launches publicly

Hedy.creator: Felienne Hermans
Hedy.history: Felienne Hermans introduced Hedy in 2020 at Leiden University to teach programming to children by adding syntax gradually, the way children learn punctuation. Level 1 has no quotes, brackets or indentation, and later levels add them step by step until the code is close to Python. It runs in the browser at hedy.org.

Sather.creator: Stephen Omohundro (ICSI)
Sather.history: Sather was developed at the International Computer Science Institute in Berkeley by a team led by Stephen Omohundro and made public in June 1991. It started from Eiffel and aimed to be simpler and faster, adding iterators and closures; it is named after Sather Tower on the Berkeley campus. #OUT creates the standard output object, and + appends the string to it.

REDUCE.creator: Anthony C. Hearn
REDUCE.history: Anthony C. Hearn began REDUCE in 1963 for calculations in particle physics, and the first paper on it as a general algebra system appeared in 1968. It is written in Standard Lisp and uses an ALGOL-like surface language. Evaluating a string at the top level displays it, so this prints Hello, World!
REDUCE.releasedEvent: First paper describing the REDUCE algebra system

AutoLISP.creator: Autodesk (based on David Betz's XLISP)
AutoLISP.history: AutoLISP is the Lisp dialect built into AutoCAD; it was derived from an early version of David Betz's XLISP and its first full version shipped with AutoCAD 2.18 in January 1986. Drafters use it to automate drawing tasks and add commands. princ writes the text to the AutoCAD command line, and the final (princ) stops the return value from being echoed.
AutoLISP.releasedEvent: AutoCAD 2.18 ships the first full version of AutoLISP

Amiga E.creator: Wouter van Oortmerssen
Amiga E.history: Wouter van Oortmerssen started Amiga E in 1991, released it publicly in 1993 and made it open source in 1997. He wrote the whole compiler in assembly language, and it was known for compiling very quickly; it became one of the most popular languages on the Amiga. WriteF prints formatted text to the console.

COMAL.creator: Børge R. Christensen & Benedict Løfstedt
COMAL.history: COMAL (Common Algorithmic Language) was created in Denmark in 1975 by Børge R. Christensen, a mathematics teacher, and Benedict Løfstedt. It took BASIC and added structured statements and named procedures in the spirit of Pascal. It was popular for teaching; in the early 1980s Irish secondary schools were supplied with Apple II computers running COMAL.

Mouse.creator: Peter Grogono
Mouse.history: Peter Grogono described Mouse in BYTE magazine in July 1979 as a very small language for microcomputers, extending MUSYS, a language he had used to control an electronic music studio. Programs are strings of single-character commands for a stack machine. A quoted string is printed, but an exclamation mark inside it means a newline, so this prints Hello, World and ends the line; $ ends the program.
Mouse.releasedEvent: Peter Grogono's article in BYTE magazine

TI-BASIC.creator: Texas Instruments
TI-BASIC.history: TI-BASIC is the BASIC-like language built into Texas Instruments graphing calculators, starting with the TI-81 in 1990. Programs are stored as tokens, so each command is entered from a menu as a single unit. On the TI-83 and TI-84 family this program displays HELLO, WORLD! on the home screen, in capitals because lowercase letters are not available by default.
TI-BASIC.releasedEvent: TI-81, the first TI graphing calculator, introduced

HyperTalk.creator: Dan Winkler (Apple)
HyperTalk.history: Dan Winkler created HyperTalk in 1987 for Bill Atkinson's HyperCard on the Macintosh. Its English-like syntax was aimed at beginners, who were called authors rather than programmers, and it influenced AppleScript and LiveCode. This handler runs when the button it belongs to is clicked, and answer shows the text in a dialog box.

Typst.creator: Laurenz Mädje & Martin Haug
Typst.history: Laurenz Mädje and Martin Haug started Typst in 2019 for their master's theses at TU Berlin, and released the compiler as open source in March 2023. It aims to be as capable as LaTeX but easier to learn, with Markdown-like markup and a built-in scripting language, and it recompiles incrementally. A file of plain text typesets a page with that text.
Typst.releasedEvent: Compiler open-sourced and public beta launched

occam.creator: David May (Inmos)
occam.history: occam was designed by David May at Inmos and released in 1983 as the native language of the transputer, a microprocessor built for parallel computing. It is based on Tony Hoare's CSP: processes share nothing and talk over channels. This version uses the course library of KRoC, the Kent occam-pi compiler, where the main process receives keyboard, screen and error channels.

MEL.creator: Alias|Wavefront
MEL.history: MEL (Maya Embedded Language) has been the scripting language of the 3D software Maya since Alias|Wavefront released Maya 1.0 in February 1998. Its syntax resembles Perl and Tcl, and most of Maya's standard commands are themselves MEL scripts. print writes the text to the Script Editor's output.

Charcoal.creator: ASCII-only & DLosc
Charcoal.history: Charcoal was designed in 2016 by the Programming Puzzles and Code Golf users ASCII-only and DLosc as a golfing language for ASCII art, which is where the name comes from. A program draws on a text canvas, where a number draws a line and an arrow sets its direction. Plain printable text is a string literal that is printed implicitly, so this program is its own output.

Dafny.creator: K. Rustan M. Leino (Microsoft Research)
Dafny.history: K. Rustan M. Leino designed Dafny at Microsoft Research, where it first appeared in 2009, to make program verification part of ordinary programming. Methods carry preconditions, postconditions and loop invariants that the verifier checks before the code compiles. Verified programs compile to C#, Java, JavaScript, Go and Python.
Dafny.releasedEvent: First appearance at Microsoft Research (Leino's lecture notes on Dafny published in 2009)

CLIPS.creator: NASA Johnson Space Center
CLIPS.history: CLIPS was developed at NASA's Johnson Space Center from 1985 to 1996 as an alternative to ART*Inference for building expert systems, and its syntax and name were inspired by Charles Forgy's OPS5. Programs are facts and if-then rules that an inference engine matches. It has been public domain since 1996; printout t writes to standard output and crlf ends the line.
CLIPS.releasedEvent: First versions developed at NASA's Johnson Space Center

CLU.creator: Barbara Liskov and her students (MIT)
CLU.history: Barbara Liskov and her students designed CLU at MIT from 1973 as the first implemented language with direct support for data abstraction; a cluster bundles a type's representation with its operations. It also introduced iterators and an exception mechanism, and its compiler was soon rewritten in CLU itself. stream$primary_output returns the standard output stream and putl writes a line to it.
CLU.releasedEvent: First appearance; a preliminary reference manual for CLU .5 was issued at MIT in January 1975

PILOT.creator: John Amsden Starkweather (UCSF)
PILOT.history: John Amsden Starkweather, a psychology professor at the University of California, San Francisco, developed PILOT in the 1960s for writing computer-assisted instruction, and it entered the public domain in 1969. Each line starts with a command letter and a colon: T types text, A accepts an answer and M matches it. Later versions ran on the Atari and Apple II home computers, and IEEE published a standard for it in 1991.
PILOT.releasedEvent: Starkweather releases an almost-complete version of PILOT

FOCAL.creator: Richard Merrill (Digital Equipment Corporation)
FOCAL.history: Richard Merrill wrote FOCAL for Digital Equipment Corporation's PDP-8 minicomputer in 1968, basing it on RAND's JOSS. Program lines are numbered as group and line, such as 01.50, and a command typed without a number runs at once. TYPE prints its items: a string in double quotes, and ! for a new line.

Labyrinth.creator: Martin Ender
Labyrinth.history: Martin Ender designed Labyrinth in 2015, a two-dimensional language whose source code is a maze of commands. At junctions the instruction pointer turns according to the sign of the top of the stack, so the shape of the program is its control flow. Each digit appends to the number on top of the stack, : duplicates it, . prints it as a character and @ ends the program.
Labyrinth.releasedEvent: Reference interpreter repository created on GitHub

Hexagony.creator: Martin Ender
Hexagony.history: Martin Ender created Hexagony in 2015, a two-dimensional language whose source code is folded onto a hexagonal grid. Its memory is a hexagonal grid too, and six instruction pointers start at the corners and wrap around the edges, with mirrors and branches redirecting them. Here letters set the current memory edge to their character code and ; prints it.
Hexagony.releasedEvent: Reference interpreter repository created on GitHub

Csound.creator: Barry Vercoe (MIT)
Csound.history: Barry Vercoe released Csound at MIT in 1985, with roots in Max Mathews's MUSIC-N programs, and it has been developed as free software by a wide community since. A .csd file holds an orchestra of instruments and a score of timed events; here the score starts instrument 1 at time 0 and prints runs when it initialises. Csound writes its own log around the greeting, and -n turns off audio output.
Csound.releasedEvent: Released by Barry Vercoe at MIT

Markdown.creator: John Gruber
Markdown.history: John Gruber released Markdown in March 2004 as a plain-text formatting syntax and a Perl script that converts it to HTML. The design goal was text that reads naturally as it is, and the biggest influence was the format of plain-text email. Plain text is a paragraph, so this file converts to a single paragraph containing Hello, World!

QML.creator: Qt Software (Nokia)
QML.history: QML came from Qt Software's development lab in Brisbane, and Matthias Ettrich presented it at LinuxTag in Berlin in June 2009 as a declarative way to build interfaces for mobile devices. A file describes a tree of objects whose properties and handlers are JavaScript expressions. Run with the Qt 6 qml tool, this prints qml: Hello, World! to the log and quits.
QML.releasedEvent: Qt Software previews QML with binaries and source; Matthias Ettrich presents it at LinuxTag in June 2009

Cypher.creator: Andrés Taylor (Neo Technology)
Cypher.history: Andrés Taylor created Cypher at Neo Technology, and its first iteration shipped in a Neo4j 1.4 milestone in June 2011 so users could query a graph without writing traversal code. Patterns draw the graph in ASCII art, with (nodes) joined by -[relationships]->. It was opened up through the openCypher project in 2015; this query returns a one-row table with the text in a greeting column.
Cypher.releasedEvent: First iteration released in Neo4j 1.4 Milestone 4

Ezhil.creator: Muthiah Annamalai
Ezhil.history: Muthiah Annamalai began Ezhil in late 2007 and announced it in July 2009, so that Tamil speakers could learn programming with keywords in their own language. It was influenced by Logo, BASIC and Python and is aimed at school students. பதிப்பி (pathippi, print) writes the string.

OPL.creator: Colly Myers (Psion)
OPL.history: Colly Myers designed OPL at Psion, and Richard Harrison and Martin Stamp implemented the first version for the original Psion Organiser in 1984, without graphics. It became built-in software on the Organiser II in 1986 and then on the Series 3 and Series 5 palmtops, and was later released as open source for Symbian. PRINT shows the text and GET waits for a key, so it stays on screen.
OPL.releasedEvent: First implementation on the original Psion Organiser

Lingo.creator: John H. Thompson (MacroMind)
Lingo.history: John H. Thompson invented Lingo at MacroMind in 1989, and it was first released with Director 2.2 to script interactive multimedia. Its verbose syntax was designed to read like spoken English, and it became the primary language of the Shockwave platform and of many CD-ROMs and kiosks. In a movie script the startMovie handler runs when the movie starts, and put shows the value in Director's Message window.

POP-11.creator: Robin Popplestone, Steve Hardy, Aaron Sloman and others (University of Sussex)
POP-11.history: POP-11, an evolution of Edinburgh University's POP-2, appeared at the University of Sussex in 1975; it became the core language of the Poplog system used to teach and research artificial intelligence. It works on an open stack, and the => operator prints values with a ** prefix. printf writes the string to standard output.
POP-11.releasedEvent: First appearance at the University of Sussex

Nial.creator: Mike Jenkins (Queen's University)
Nial.history: Mike Jenkins developed Nial, the Nested Interactive Array Language, at Queen's University in Canada from about 1981, building on the array theory of Trenchard More. It belongs to the APL family but uses a more traditional, word-based syntax, and Jenkins founded Nial Systems in 1982 to market the Q'Nial implementation. write displays the picture of an array on the screen, and the picture of a string is its text.

XPL0.creator: Peter J. R. Boyle
XPL0.history: Peter J. R. Boyle created XPL0 in 1976 for the 6502 microprocessor as a small, fast, block-structured alternative to BASIC. It is based on PL/0, the example compiler in Niklaus Wirth's book Algorithms + Data Structures = Programs. Here code Text=12 binds the name Text to built-in routine 12, which outputs a string, and 0 sends it to the display screen.

Monkey X.creator: Mark Sibly (Blitz Research)
Monkey X.history: Blitz Research released Monkey on 1 March 2011, a language by Mark Sibly with syntax similar to BlitzMax that translates its source into code for each target, from Windows and Mac OS X to iOS, Android, HTML5 and Flash. Development moved to Monkey2 in 2015, and the community fork Cerberus X carries on the original. Every program's main module has a Main function, where execution begins.

SVG.creator: W3C SVG Working Group (editor Jon Ferraiolo)
SVG.history: The W3C's SVG Working Group published Scalable Vector Graphics 1.0 as a Recommendation in September 2001, an XML vocabulary for shapes, paths and text. Every modern browser renders it directly, and it is also the format icon sets and many drawing programs export. Opened in a browser, this file draws Hello, World! as text on a 200 by 40 canvas.
SVG.releasedEvent: SVG 1.0 published as a W3C Recommendation

SPARQL.creator: W3C RDF Data Access Working Group (editors Eric Prud'hommeaux and Andy Seaborne)
SPARQL.history: SPARQL became a W3C Recommendation in January 2008 as the standard way to query RDF, the graph data model of the Semantic Web, by matching triple patterns. SPARQL 1.1 followed in 2013 and added expressions in the SELECT clause, which this query uses. With an empty pattern it returns one row whose greeting column holds Hello, World!
SPARQL.releasedEvent: SPARQL Query Language for RDF published as a W3C Recommendation

Terraform.creator: Mitchell Hashimoto (HashiCorp)
Terraform.history: Mitchell Hashimoto announced Terraform at HashiCorp in July 2014 as a tool for describing infrastructure across many cloud providers as code. Configurations are written in the HashiCorp Configuration Language (HCL), and terraform plan previews changes before apply makes them. This configuration creates no resources; terraform apply lists the greeting output with the value Hello, World! after applying.
Terraform.releasedEvent: Terraform announced and released by HashiCorp

Haml.creator: Hampton Catlin
Haml.history:
Hampton Catlin created Haml (HTML Abstraction Markup Language) in 2006 because he was tired of typing HTML templates by hand, and it was first used in production at Unspace Interactive. Indentation replaces closing tags, and a % sign starts an element. This template renders

Hello, World!

.

Sass.creator: Hampton Catlin; developed by Natalie Weizenbaum
Sass.history: Sass was designed by Hampton Catlin and developed by Natalie Weizenbaum, first appearing in 2006 with an indented syntax similar to Haml; the brace-based SCSS syntax followed. It adds variables, nesting and mixins to CSS. This file uses the original indented syntax, and Dart Sass prints the message with a location prefix, like hello.sass:1 Debug: Hello, World!

Pug.creator: TJ Holowaychuk
Pug.history:
TJ Holowaychuk started the Node.js template engine as Jade in 2010. It was renamed Pug for version 2 because Jade is a registered trademark. A line starts with a tag name and the rest is its text, so this template renders

Hello, World!

.

DOT.creator: Eleftherios Koutsofios and Stephen North (AT&T Bell Laboratories)
DOT.history: DOT is the graph language of the dot layout program from AT&T Bell Laboratories, described in Eleftherios Koutsofios and Stephen North's 1991 report Drawing graphs with dot; dot succeeded an earlier program called dag. It is now the input format of the open-source Graphviz tools. Rendered with dot -Tsvg, this graph is a single node labelled Hello, World!
DOT.releasedEvent: Koutsofios and North publish the AT&T Bell Laboratories report "Drawing graphs with dot"

NetLogo.creator: Uri Wilensky (Northwestern University)
NetLogo.history: Uri Wilensky wrote NetLogo in 1999, and it has been developed since at Northwestern University's Center for Connected Learning and Computer-Based Modeling. It follows Logo's low-threshold, no-ceiling idea, with turtles, patches and links acting as agents in simulations of natural and social systems. Typed in the Command Center, show prints the value with the agent in front: observer: "Hello, World!"

ALGOL W.creator: Niklaus Wirth and Tony Hoare
ALGOL W.history: Niklaus Wirth and Tony Hoare based ALGOL W on their proposal for ALGOL X, the planned successor to ALGOL 60, and it first appeared in 1966. Wirth supervised a widely distributed compiler for the IBM System/360 at Stanford, written in his ALGOL-like PL360. write prints its arguments as a line; awe is a modern compiler for the language.
ALGOL W.releasedEvent: First appeared, based on Wirth and Hoare's proposal for ALGOL X

ISLISP.creator: ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 22/WG 16
ISLISP.history: ISLISP was standardised by the ISO working group SC22/WG16 and published as ISO/IEC 13816:1997, with a revision in 2007. It aims to be a small core of what Lisp dialects agree on, and the text of its specification was dedicated to the public domain. format writes to the stream returned by (standard-output), and ~% outputs a newline.

Asymptote.creator: Andy Hammerlindl, John C. Bowman and Tom Prince
Asymptote.history: Andy Hammerlindl, John C. Bowman and Tom Prince created Asymptote in 2004, a descriptive vector graphics language influenced by MetaPost that typesets its labels with LaTeX. It is used for mathematical and technical drawings, and later versions extended it to three dimensions. write prints its argument to the terminal.
Asymptote.releasedEvent: First appeared; the SourceForge project was registered on 23 September 2004

Metafont.creator: Donald Knuth
Metafont.history: Donald Knuth began work on Metafont in 1977 as the font companion to his TeX typesetting system, produced a first version in 1979 and replaced it with an entirely new system in 1984, the one still in use. Its programs describe the shapes of letters and are compiled to bitmap fonts for a given printer. Run with mf, message shows the text on the terminal after the program's banner.
Metafont.releasedEvent: First version produced (rewritten as the current Metafont in 1984)

CFEngine.creator: Mark Burgess (Oslo University)
CFEngine.history: Mark Burgess wrote CFEngine in 1993 as a post-doctoral fellow at Oslo University to automate the workstations of a physics department, and his work on it led to promise theory. Policies declare desired states that cf-agent converges towards. This sample uses CFEngine 3 syntax, where a bundle named main runs by default and a reports promise prints R: Hello, World!
CFEngine.releasedEvent: First version, written by Mark Burgess at Oslo University

Refal.creator: Valentin Turchin
Refal.history: Valentin Turchin conceived Refal in 1966 as a theoretical tool, and the first implementation appeared in 1968; later versions include Refal-2, Refal-5, Refal-6 and Refal+. Functions are defined by sentences that match patterns in their argument. In Refal-5, $ENTRY Go marks the entry point and Prout prints its argument and expands to nothing.
Refal.releasedEvent: First implementation (conceived in 1966 as a theoretical tool)

Virgil.creator: Ben L. Titzer
Virgil.history: Ben L. Titzer introduced Virgil in a 2006 OOPSLA paper; it was first designed for embedded systems, particularly microcontrollers. Today it blends classes, functions, tuples, type parameters and algebraic data types, and compiles to native executables, JVM jar files and WebAssembly. The compiler and runtime are written in Virgil itself; System.puts writes the string.
Virgil.releasedEvent: Introduced in Titzer's OOPSLA 2006 paper "Virgil: Objects on the Head of a Pin"

Dialog.creator: Linus Åkesson
Dialog.history: Linus Åkesson announced Dialog in November 2018, a language for interactive fiction that combines the rule-based style of Prolog with ideas from Inform 7; his game Tethered was the first published with it. Stories compile to the Z-machine or to his own Å-machine. Execution starts at the (program entry point) rule, and plain text in a rule body is printed.

CUE.creator: Marcel van Lohuizen
CUE.history: Marcel van Lohuizen started CUE (Configure, Unify, Execute) as open source in 2018; its roots lie in GCL, the configuration language Google used for Borg, the predecessor of Kubernetes. It is a superset of JSON for validating and defining configuration. cue export prints it as JSON, an object whose greeting field is Hello, World!
CUE.releasedEvent: Initial commit of the open-source CUE repository

LilyPond.creator: Han-Wen Nienhuys and Jan Nieuwenhuizen
LilyPond.history: Han-Wen Nienhuys and Jan Nieuwenhuizen started LilyPond in 1996 after abandoning MPP, their preprocessor for MusiXTeX, and version 1.0 in 1998 brought its own Feta music font. The name refers to the Rosegarden project and to a friend named Suzanne, a Hebrew name meaning lily. A top-level markup block typesets Hello, World! on a page of its own.
LilyPond.releasedEvent: First 0.0.x releases (git history shows release 0.0.1 on 9 October 1996)

Austral.creator: Fernando Borretti
Austral.history: Fernando Borretti introduced Austral in December 2022 as a small systems language with linear types and capability-based security, with a bootstrapping compiler in OCaml that emits C. Its syntax resembles Ada. The entry point is chosen on the command line with --entrypoint=Hello:main, and main returns an ExitCode.

Rhombus.creator: Racket team (Matthew Flatt, Robert Bruce Findler, Sam Tobin-Hochstadt and others)
Rhombus.history: Rhombus is built on Racket by the Racket team, with Matthew Flatt among its major contributors, and reached version 1.0 in June 2026. It keeps Racket's macro system and extensibility but uses a conventional infix syntax instead of parentheses. The #lang rhombus line selects the language, and print writes the string without quotes.

AMPL.creator: Robert Fourer, David Gay and Brian Kernighan (Bell Laboratories)
AMPL.history: Robert Fourer, David Gay and Brian Kernighan designed and implemented AMPL (A Mathematical Programming Language) at Bell Laboratories in 1985, and a paper describing it appeared in Management Science in 1990. Models are written in algebraic notation close to the mathematics and handed to separate solvers. Besides model declarations, AMPL has script commands such as printf, which uses C-style format strings.
AMPL.releasedEvent: AMPL designed and implemented at Bell Laboratories

ParaSail.creator: S. Tucker Taft (AdaCore)
ParaSail.history: Tucker Taft, lead designer of Ada 95, began designing ParaSail (Parallel Specification and Implementation Language) in September 2009 and documented the work on a blog, where the first alpha compiler and virtual machine were announced in October 2011. The language has no pointers and no global variables, so the compiler can evaluate expressions in parallel safely. The IO object is passed in as a parameter instead of being global.
ParaSail.releasedEvent: Alpha release of the ParaSail compiler and virtual machine announced

Ecstasy.creator: Cameron Purdy and Gene Gleyzer
Ecstasy.history: Cameron Purdy and Gene Gleyzer, who earlier co-founded Tangosol, designed Ecstasy (also called XTC) for cloud and serverless applications; the project blog introduced it in April 2019. Code runs inside nested containers, and a module receives resources such as the console only by injection, as @Inject does here. The xtc tool builds and runs the module.
Ecstasy.releasedEvent: Ecstasy introduced on the project blog, with its source to be released under the Apache 2.0 license

Egison.creator: Satoshi Egi
Egison.history: Satoshi Egi released Egison on Hackage in May 2011 to express pattern matching against non-free data types such as sets and multisets directly, without spelling out how to search them. Early versions used an S-expression syntax; this sample uses the Haskell-like syntax of Egison 4, released in 2020.

Maude.creator: José Meseguer, Steven Eker, Manuel Clavel, Francisco Durán, Patrick Lincoln, Narciso Martí-Oliet and José Quesada (SRI International)
Maude.history: Maude grew out of José Meseguer's work on rewriting logic at SRI International, and Maude 1.0 was announced in January 1999 as a successor in spirit to Joseph Goguen's OBJ3. Programs are equations and rewrite rules, which also makes Maude a tool for specifying and model checking systems. The red command reduces a term in the STRING module and prints result String: "Hello, World!".
Maude.releasedEvent: José Meseguer announces the Maude 1.0 release

mIRC scripting.creator: Khaled Mardam-Bey
mIRC scripting.history: Khaled Mardam-Bey released the first public version of the Windows IRC client mIRC on 28 February 1995, and its scripting language, in his words, grew organically rather than being designed. Scripts add aliases, popup menus and handlers for IRC events, and were used to write bots and full client add-ons. Loaded as a remote script, this defines a /hello command that shows Hello, World! in the active window.
mIRC scripting.releasedEvent: First appeared with the mIRC client, whose first public version was released on 28 February 1995

ECL.creator: David Bayliss (Seisint, later LexisNexis Risk Solutions)
ECL.history: David Bayliss designed ECL (Enterprise Control Language) in 2000 as an in-house tool at Seisint, and it became public in June 2011 when LexisNexis Risk Solutions open-sourced the HPCC Systems platform. ECL is declarative and free of side effects, which lets the platform run programs in parallel across a cluster. OUTPUT writes the string as a result of the workunit.
ECL.releasedEvent: LexisNexis announces HPCC Systems and ECL as open source

Gremlin.creator: Marko A. Rodriguez (TinkerPop)
Gremlin.history: Marko A. Rodriguez started the TinkerPop project in October 2009 and released Gremlin 0.1 on 25 December 2009. Gremlin queries chain steps that walk a graph, and the same traversal can run on many graph databases. This uses current TinkerPop 3 syntax in the Gremlin Console: inject puts the string into an empty traversal, and after echoing the graph and g the console prints ==>Hello, World!

Kitten.creator: Jon Purdy
Kitten.history: Jon Purdy started Kitten in December 2011 as a statically typed concatenative language: functions take their arguments from a stack, as in Forth and Factor, but it is statically typed, and its implementation is written in Haskell. The string is pushed onto the stack and say prints it with a newline.
Kitten.releasedEvent: Initial commit of the Kitten repository

Potion.creator: why the lucky stiff
Potion.history: The Ruby writer why the lucky stiff checked in the first Potion code in December 2008, a small language whose objects and mixins sit on a virtual machine heavily based on Lua's, with a JIT to x86 and x86-64. The perl11 project keeps the official repository going until _why returns. Messages follow the receiver, so the string is sent print.

ooc.creator: Amos Wenger
ooc.history: Amos Wenger wrote the first ooc compiler in 2009 as a student at EPFL, a source-to-source translator from a Java-like language to C, so he would not have to write a class project in C. He then rewrote it, and the self-hosted compiler rock still generates C99. Strings have a println method, so the greeting is the receiver here.
ooc.releasedEvent: First ooc compiler written by Amos Wenger at EPFL

Bicep.creator: Microsoft (Azure)
Bicep.history: Microsoft published the first alpha of Bicep in August 2020 as a simpler way to write Azure Resource Manager templates, which are otherwise long JSON documents. Bicep files compile to ARM JSON and describe resources, parameters and outputs. Deployed, this file creates no resources and lists an output named greeting with the value Hello, World!

Rego.creator: Tim Hinrichs, Torin Sandall and Teemu Koponen (Styra)
Rego.history: Tim Hinrichs, Torin Sandall and Teemu Koponen created Open Policy Agent at Styra, and its policy language Rego shipped in OPA v0.1.0 in July 2016. Rego is inspired by Datalog and extended to query structured documents such as JSON. The := operator in this sample is the current form of rule assignment; opa eval --format raw -d hello.rego data.hello.greeting prints Hello, World!
Rego.releasedEvent: Open Policy Agent v0.1.0 released with the Rego language

Yacas.creator: Ayal Pinkus and Serge Winitzki
Yacas.history: Ayal Pinkus started Yacas (Yet Another Computer Algebra System) in early 1999, and Serge Winitzki became a main co-developer. A small C++ kernel evaluates a rule-based scripting language in which most of the mathematics is written. Echo prints a string without quotation marks and adds a newline; in the interactive shell it then shows Out> True.

KCL.creator: Ant Group
KCL.history: Ant Group open-sourced KCL in May 2022 after using it for platform engineering in production, and it became a CNCF Sandbox project in September 2023. Its Python-like syntax adds schemas and constraints for writing and validating large Kubernetes and cloud configurations. Running kcl hello.k prints the result as YAML: hello: Hello, World!
KCL.releasedEvent: v0.4.2-alpha.1, the first GitHub release after Ant Group open-sourced KCL

Expect.creator: Don Libes (NIST)
Expect.history: Don Libes wrote Expect at NIST in 1990 and described it at the Summer 1990 USENIX Conference. It extends Tcl with spawn, expect and send, so a script can drive programs that insist on a person typing, such as passwd, telnet or ftp sessions. send_user writes to the user's terminal instead of the spawned process.
Expect.releasedEvent: Libes presents "Expect: Curing Those Uncontrollable Fits of Interaction" at the Summer 1990 USENIX Conference

Taxi.creator: Sean Heber
Taxi.history: Sean Heber conceived Taxi on 21 June 2005 and released it six days later. Values are passengers that a taxi picks up and drops off at places on a fixed map of Townsburg, driving by turn-by-turn directions, and the taxi needs fuel paid for by fares. Dropping a passenger at the Post Office prints it, and the program ends at the Taxi Garage.

Ur/Web.creator: Adam Chlipala
Ur/Web.history: Adam Chlipala made the first public release of Ur/Web in October 2008, built on Ur, his functional language in the tradition of ML and Haskell with a richer type system, plus a special standard library for web applications backed by SQL databases. Well-typed programs cannot suffer code injection, return invalid HTML or contain dead links inside the application, and the compiled server runs without garbage collection. main returns an XML page, so this program serves a page headed Hello, World!
Ur/Web.releasedEvent: Initial public release, urweb-20081025, an alpha under a BSD license

UnrealScript.creator: Tim Sweeney (Epic Games)
UnrealScript.history: Tim Sweeney created UnrealScript as the scripting language of the Unreal Engine, and it first shipped with the game Unreal in May 1998. It was object-oriented and similar to Java, and Epic carried it through three engine generations before announcing at the 2012 Game Developers Conference that Unreal Engine 4 would drop it in favor of C++. A commandlet is a small program run from the command line with ucc, and log writes the line to the log.
UnrealScript.releasedEvent: First appeared with Unreal Engine 1 and the game Unreal

Jack.creator: Noam Nisan and Shimon Schocken
Jack.history: Noam Nisan and Shimon Schocken designed Jack for The Elements of Computing Systems (MIT Press, 2005), the book behind the Nand to Tetris course, in which students build a whole computer starting from NAND gates. Jack is a simple object-based language with Java-like syntax, and students write the compiler that translates it to the course's virtual machine. Output.printString belongs to the small Jack operating system they also implement.
Jack.releasedEvent: Specified in The Elements of Computing Systems (MIT Press)

HLA.creator: Randall Hyde
HLA.history: Randall Hyde began writing HLA (High Level Assembly) at UC Riverside in the fall of 1996 and released the first prototype, version 1.0, in September 1999. It adds high-level declarations and control structures to x86 assembly so that beginners can start from familiar ground, and it is the language of his book The Art of Assembly Language. stdout.put comes from the HLA Standard Library.
HLA.releasedEvent: First prototype of HLA released as version 1.0

Cowgol.creator: David Given
Cowgol.history: David Given started Cowgol as a type-safe, Ada-inspired language for very small systems such as the 6502 and Z80, with the goal of a compiler that can rebuild itself on an 8-bit micro. The first demo release in September 2017 came as a bootable disk image for a BBC Micro emulator. The current Cowgol 2.0 compiler is written in Cowgol and targets CP/M, the BBC Micro, Fuzix, DOS and Linux; this sample uses the current Cowgol 2.0 syntax.
Cowgol.releasedEvent: Cowgol 0.0.1, the first demo release, on GitHub

MDL.creator: Gerald Sussman, Carl Hewitt, Chris Reeve and Bruce Daniels (MIT)
MDL.history: MDL, also called Muddle, was developed at MIT from 1971 by Gerald Sussman, Carl Hewitt, Chris Reeve, Bruce Daniels and others as a descendant of Lisp. The original Zork was written in MDL, and in 1980 Marc Blank and Joel Berez adapted a subset of it into ZIL, which Infocom used for its games. Calls use angle brackets, PRINC prints the string and CRLF ends the line.

Skew.creator: Evan Wallace
Skew.history: Evan Wallace created Skew as a web-first, cross-platform language whose optimizing compiler emits readable JavaScript and C#. The compiler is bootstrapped, so it is written in Skew and compiles itself, and code compiles about as fast as a browser refresh. @entry marks the entry point, and dynamic gives untyped access to JavaScript globals such as console.
Skew.releasedEvent: skew 0.1.0, the first npm release with the compiler (a 0.0.0 entry from April 2014 holds no compiler)

Smali.creator: Ben Gruver (JesusFreke)
Smali.history: Ben Gruver released smali, an assembler for the dex format of Android's Dalvik virtual machine, in June 2009, and its disassembler baksmali followed later that month; the names are Icelandic for assembler and disassembler. This program loads System.out into a register and calls println on it.
Smali.releasedEvent: First release of the smali assembler

Jinja.creator: Armin Ronacher
Jinja.history: Armin Ronacher published Jinja on PyPI in July 2006, and the rewritten Jinja2 2.0 followed in July 2008. It is now maintained by the Pallets project. Text between double braces is an expression whose value is printed, so this template renders Hello, World!
Jinja.releasedEvent: Jinja 0.8, the earliest release on PyPI

Xojo.creator: Andrew Barry (later Xojo, Inc.)
Xojo.history: Andrew Barry marketed CrossBasic as shareware; Geoff Perlman's FYI Software bought it, a public beta was released in April 1996, the name became REALbasic because CrossBasic was trademarked elsewhere, and REALbasic 1.0 was introduced at Macworld Expo in 1998; the company and product were renamed Xojo on 4 June 2013. It is an object-oriented BASIC whose IDE builds desktop, web and console applications from one code base. This is the Run event of a console application, a project type of later versions (this form is documented for REALbasic 5.5): Print writes the line and Quit ends the program.
Xojo.releasedEvent: Public beta of the BASIC environment that became REALbasic and later Xojo

RPL.creator: Hewlett-Packard (William C. Wickes and others)
RPL.history: RPL (Reverse Polish Lisp) originated at Hewlett-Packard's Corvallis, Oregon, facility in 1984, and the HP-28C of 1986 was the first calculator that let users program in it. It works on a stack in reverse Polish notation, and programs are written between « and ». MSGBOX, available on later models such as the HP 48gII, shows the string in a message box.
RPL.releasedEvent: HP-28C, the first calculator programmable by users in RPL

AmbientTalk.creator: Tom Van Cutsem, Stijn Mostinckx, Jessie Dedecker and Wolfgang De Meuter (Vrije Universiteit Brussel)
AmbientTalk.history: Tom Van Cutsem, Stijn Mostinckx, Jessie Dedecker and Wolfgang De Meuter designed AmbientTalk at the Software Languages Lab of the Vrije Universiteit Brussel in 2006 for ambient-oriented programming, in which devices in a mobile ad hoc network find each other and cooperate. Its concurrency features, futures and event-loop concurrency, are founded on the actor model and were largely influenced by the E language. system.println writes to the console.
AmbientTalk.releasedEvent: First appeared at the Software Languages Lab, Vrije Universiteit Brussel

Avail.creator: Mark van Gulik and Todd L Smith
Avail.history: Mark van Gulik began Avail (Advanced Value And Identity Language) around 1993, Todd L Smith later joined him, and the first version was released on 28 April 2014. Without the standard library module Avail there is no syntax beyond module headers; types, arithmetic and control structures all come from the library. The module name must match the file name, and running the Greet entry point prints the greeting.

PowerBASIC.creator: Robert "Bob" Zale
PowerBASIC.history: Robert "Bob" Zale designed BASIC/Z, which Borland sold as Turbo Basic from 1987, and the compiler returned under the name PowerBASIC in May 1990. Later versions, PB/CC for console programs and PB/Win for Windows, compile to native executables; this sample uses the PB/CC form, in which PBMain is the entry point, and Waitkey$ keeps the console window open until a key is pressed.
PowerBASIC.releasedEvent: PowerBASIC 2.0, the initial release as successor to Borland's Turbo Basic 1.1

XML.creator: W3C XML Working Group (editors Tim Bray, Jean Paoli and C. M. Sperberg-McQueen)
XML.history: XML 1.0 became a W3C Recommendation on 10 February 1998, edited by Tim Bray, Jean Paoli and C. M. Sperberg-McQueen as a subset of SGML for use on the web. A document has a single root element and any tag names the author chooses; this one is a greeting element containing Hello, World!
XML.releasedEvent: XML 1.0 published as a W3C Recommendation

JSON.creator: Douglas Crockford
JSON.history: Douglas Crockford specified JSON in the early 2000s, and he and Chip Morningstar sent the first JSON message in April 2001; the JSON.org website launched the same year. It was first standardized in 2013 as ECMA-404. The file is an object whose message member holds Hello, World!
JSON.releasedEvent: JSON.org website launched; the first JSON message was sent in April 2001

TOML.creator: Tom Preston-Werner
TOML.history: Tom Preston-Werner created TOML, whose name stands for Tom's Obvious Minimal Language, as a configuration format that maps unambiguously to a hash table. Version 0.1.0 came out on 17 March 2013. The file sets the key message to the string Hello, World!

reStructuredText.creator: David Goodger
reStructuredText.history: David Goodger found Zope's StructuredText in late 1999 while looking for a way to document Python modules, and reworked it into reStructuredText; the first draft of the specification went to the Python Doc-SIG in November 2000 and the first release followed in June 2001. In 2002 the project merged into Docutils. An underlined line becomes a title, so this file renders the heading Hello, World!
reStructuredText.releasedEvent: Project website and first project release rolled out

AsciiDoc.creator: Stuart Rackham
AsciiDoc.history: Stuart Rackham created AsciiDoc in 2002 and released his Python processor for it in November 2002. A line starting with = is the document title, so this file renders the title Hello, World!
AsciiDoc.releasedEvent: First release of Stuart Rackham's AsciiDoc Python processor

Org.creator: Carsten Dominik
Org.history: Carsten Dominik started Org mode for GNU Emacs in 2003, originally to organize his own life and work. Its plain-text format is built around outlines of headlines. A line starting with an asterisk is a top-level headline, so this file is an outline with the single heading Hello, World!
Org.releasedEvent: Initial release (year given in Wikipedia's infobox)

Textile.creator: Dean Allen
Textile.history: Dean Allen developed Textile in 2002 and described it as a humane web text generator. A block signature such as h1. at the start of a paragraph chooses the HTML element. This file converts to an h1 heading reading Hello, World!

RTF.creator: Richard Brodie, Charles Simonyi and David Luebbert (Microsoft)
RTF.history: Richard Brodie, Charles Simonyi and David Luebbert of the Microsoft Word team created the Rich Text Format, and the first reader and writer shipped in 1987 with Word 3.0 for Macintosh. Microsoft developed the format until 2008. A document is a group in braces that starts with \rtf1, and word processors open this file as one paragraph reading Hello, World!
RTF.releasedEvent: First RTF reader and writer shipped with Microsoft Word 3.0 for Macintosh

SPSS.creator: Norman H. Nie, Dale H. Bent and C. Hadlai Hull
SPSS.history: Norman H. Nie, Dale H. Bent and C. Hadlai Hull released the first version of SPSS, the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences, in 1968; IBM now sells it as IBM SPSS Statistics. Analyses are written as commands that each end with a period. ECHO writes its quoted text to the output log, which shows Hello, World!

Texinfo.creator: Richard Stallman and Robert Chassell
Texinfo.history: Richard Stallman created Texinfo, the documentation format of the GNU Project, first released in February 1986, and Robert Chassell helped him write the first translator to Info files in Emacs Lisp. makeinfo --plaintext turns this file into the top heading Hello, World! underlined with asterisks.

X10.creator: Kemal Ebcioğlu, Saravanan Arumugam, Vijay Saraswat and Vivek Sarkar (IBM)
X10.history: IBM developed X10 at the Thomas J. Watson Research Center as part of the PERCS project, funded by DARPA's High Productivity Computing Systems program. Its primary authors were Kemal Ebcioğlu, Saravanan Arumugam, Vijay Saraswat and Vivek Sarkar. The sample follows the X10 2.x style with def and Rail.
X10.releasedEvent: First appeared at IBM's Thomas J. Watson Research Center

MQL4.creator: MetaQuotes Software
MQL4.history: MetaQuotes released MetaTrader 4 on 1 July 2005 after two years of development, together with the MQL4 IDE for writing automated trading strategies. The C-like language is used for expert advisors, custom indicators and scripts that run inside the trading terminal. In current MQL4, OnStart is the event handler of a script, and Print enters Hello, World! in the Expert Advisor log.
MQL4.releasedEvent: MetaTrader 4 released with the MQL4 IDE

Jactl.creator: James Crawford
Jactl.history: James Crawford wrote Jactl for the JVM so that Java applications could let their users customise behaviour through a secure, locked-down scripting language; its syntax combines parts of Java, Groovy and Perl. A built-in suspend and resume mechanism based on continuations means a script never blocks the thread it runs on.
Jactl.releasedEvent: Jactl 1.0.0 published on GitHub (first GitHub release)

Latitude.creator: Silvio Mayolo
Latitude.history: Silvio Mayolo designed Latitude as a prototype-oriented language with no classes, only objects that are cloned from other objects. Its syntax borrows from Ruby, Smalltalk and Erlang, and statements end with a full stop. It also offers first-class scope objects and full continuations through callCC.
Latitude.releasedEvent: Tag v0.1.0, "Initial release of the Latitude language"

AsciiDots.creator: Aaron Janse
AsciiDots.history: Aaron Janse created AsciiDots in 2017 as an esoteric language based on ASCII art. Dots, written as periods, travel down ASCII-art paths and undergo operations along the way, and the project was featured on Hacker News and Motherboard. This one-line program from the project's samples prints Hello, World!.
AsciiDots.releasedEvent: GitHub repository created (listed under 2017 on esolangs.org)

Mint.creator: Szikszai Gusztáv
Mint.history: Szikszai Gusztáv created Mint, which its project describes as a refreshing programming language for the front-end web; version 0.0.0 appeared on GitHub on 18 March 2018. User interfaces are written as components whose render functions return HTML-like markup. The Main component is mounted on the page, so its render function shows Hello, World! in the browser.

Soufflé.creator: Oracle Labs
Soufflé.history: Oracle Labs made Soufflé, a Datalog variant for static program analysis, open source on 8 March 2016; the 2016 paper Soufflé: On Synthesis of Program Analyzers is by Herbert Jordan, Bernhard Scholz and Pavle Subotić. It can interpret a program or synthesize a parallel C++ version of it, and the Doop Java pointer analysis was ported to it. The output directive with IO=stdout prints the greeting relation, whose only fact is Hello, World!, to the terminal.
Soufflé.releasedEvent: Oracle Labs made Soufflé open source

Hush.creator: Gabriel Bastos
Hush.history: Gabriel Bastos created Hush, a Unix shell scripting language based on the Lua programming language. Its documentation describes it as closer to a general purpose programming language with first-class shell capabilities than to a traditional shell. Output goes through the standard library, so std.print writes Hello, World!.

Fortress.creator: Guy L. Steele Jr. and others (Sun Labs)
Fortress.history: Fortress was developed at Sun Labs by a team that included Guy L. Steele Jr. Version 1.0 of the Fortress Language Specification was released in April 2008, and the last implementation release, 1.0_5033, is dated 7 September 2011. A program is a component that exports Executable, and its run function prints Hello, World!.

4D.creator: Laurent Ribardière
4D.history: Laurent Ribardière created 4D, known as Silver Surfer during early development, in 1984; its public release for the Macintosh followed in 1987. The product is published by the French company 4D SAS and combines a database with its own programming language. ALERT shows Hello, World! in a dialog box with an OK button.
4D.releasedEvent: Official public release for the Macintosh

OpenEdge ABL.creator: Data Language Corporation (now Progress Software)
OpenEdge ABL.history: The language was designed in 1981 as an architecture-independent language with an integrated database system, and the company, then called Data Language, released its first commercial version of PROGRESS for Unix in 1984. It was called PROGRESS or Progress 4GL up to version 9 and was renamed OpenEdge Advanced Business Language in 2006. DISPLAY shows Hello, World! in a frame on the screen.
OpenEdge ABL.releasedEvent: Data Language released the first commercial version of PROGRESS ADE for Unix

PowerBuilder.creator: Computer Solutions Inc. (later Powersoft)
PowerBuilder.history: PowerBuilder was originated by Computer Solutions Inc., which renamed itself Powersoft in 1990, and version 1.0 was released in July 1991; it is now developed by Appeon. Applications are written in the PowerScript language together with the DataWindow component. Placed in an event script such as the application's Open event, this statement shows a message box titled Greeting containing Hello, World!.

Lil.creator: John Earnest
Lil.history: John Earnest designed Lil as the scripting language of Decker, which its repository calls a multimedia sketchpad; Decker was first tagged as v1.0 on 28 October 2022. Lil statements are always expressions, and the language has built-in query statements (select, update, extract) for tables. Run with the Lilt command-line interpreter, print writes Hello, World! to standard output.
Lil.releasedEvent: Decker v1.0 tagged ("initial checkin for release"), shipping Lil and the Lilt interpreter

JScript.creator: Microsoft
JScript.history: JScript is Microsoft's dialect of JavaScript (ECMAScript), first supported in Internet Explorer 3.0, released in August 1996. Besides the browser, it runs under the Windows Script Host, where the WScript object is available. WScript.Echo prints Hello, World! to the console under cscript.exe and shows it in a message box under wscript.exe.

Toit.creator: Toitware ApS
Toit.history: Toit was built at the Danish company Toitware by a team of former Google employees whose earlier work included the V8 and Dart virtual machines; its compiler sources carry a 2018 Toitware copyright. In November 2021 the compiler, virtual machine and standard libraries were released on GitHub under LGPL-2.1. Programs start at a main: block and are run with toit run.
Toit.releasedEvent: Compiler, virtual machine and standard libraries open-sourced on GitHub

dBase.creator: C. Wayne Ratliff
dBase.history: C. Wayne Ratliff, a contractor at JPL, ported the JPLDIS database program to PTDOS on his kit-built IMSAI 8080 and called it Vulcan. Ashton-Tate licensed the CP/M port and sold it as dBASE II, and other companies built their own variations of its language, the xBase products such as Clipper and FoxPro. The ? command starts a new line and displays Hello, World!. Wikipedia gives 1978 in its text and 1979 in its infobox.

Visual FoxPro.creator: Microsoft
Visual FoxPro.history: Visual FoxPro descends from FoxPro, an xBase dialect that came to Microsoft when Fox Technologies merged with it in 1992, and version 3.0 in 1995 was the first Visual release. Version 9.0, released in December 2004, was the last, and its extended support ended in January 2015. MESSAGEBOX shows Hello, World! in a standard Windows message box.

SourcePawn.creator: AlliedModders
SourcePawn.history: SourcePawn is the language of SourceMod, the AlliedModders server modification for Valve's Source engine, and is derived from the Pawn embedded scripting language. AlliedModders lists its additions over Pawn as functions passed as objects, natively packed strings and dynamic local variables. Plugins are compiled to bytecode, and OnPluginStart runs when the plugin loads, printing Hello, World! to the server console.
SourcePawn.releasedEvent: First public SourceMod builds with SourcePawn scripting

Uniface.creator: Inside Automation (Bodo Douqué, Frits Kress)
Uniface.history: Uniface began in the Netherlands in 1984 as UNIS, built by Inside Automation, a company headed by Bodo Douqué with Frits Kress as technical director. Product and company were renamed Uniface by 1986, and it later passed to Compuware in 1994 and Rocket Software in 2021. Proc code such as message runs inside triggers and shows Hello, World! in the message frame.
Uniface.releasedEvent: Uniface Version 3, the first public release

Clarion.creator: Bruce Barrington
Clarion.history: Bruce Barrington, one of the founders of HBO & Company, created Clarion with a small team, and it was first released in April 1986. Development later moved through Jensen & Partners International, Clarion International and SoftVelocity, which sells the current Windows version. Statements are indented because column one is reserved for labels, and MESSAGE shows Hello, World! in a dialog box.
